4	SUPERTRAINING
5	One more feature should be noted. I f the given means do not elicit an adequate training effect, then increase 
6	m work capacity becomes more a factor o f specialised exercise than training volume and then only if it is executed 
7	by training at or near personal maximum levels. It should be pointed out that the execution o f specialised 
8	exercises in training at near maximal intensity (as advocated by Bulgarian experts) should be regarded as an 
9	advanced strategy, a method which cannot be acknowledged as being universally appropriate. This would imply 
10	not only rejecting the principles of the rational structuring of training based on research into training methods, but 
11	also a return to the original concepts from which these began.
12	Thus, the problem of establishing scientifically the means of sport training is far from being solved and the 
13	current tendency to increase the volume of the training load should not detract from its significance and turn the 
14	attention of specialists away from its in-depth study.
15	If a logical sequence is to be recommended as a practical solution to the problem of improving the 
16	effectiveness of special strength training methods, then it should be laid down as follows:
17	1. Regime —
18	2. Means — ► 3. Methods — ► 4. System — ► 5. Volume
19	From this scheme it follows that the means of special strength training should be selected on the basis of 
20	quantitative descriptions of the motor specificity of the given sport and thereby provide an adequate regime of 
21	work for the body. The basic criterion for this is a guarantee of a definite training effect for the given level of 
22	special fitness.
23	The next step is to determine a suitable method of using the means based not only on the specific motor 
24	regimes of the given sport, but also on factors such as one’s level of fitness and the tasks of the current stage of 
25	training. Of great potential for perfecting the methods of special strength training, is the principle o f systematic 
26	application o f means to produce the necessary cumulative training effect.
27	Finally, attaining the necessary level of special strength training depends on the volume of the special work, 
28	the optimal magnitude of which should be determined by the stage and current tasks of the athlete's preparation, 
29	the competition calendar and the intensity of the load.
30	This scheme emphasizes that, to rely on any one parameter of the load for achieving any given potential is 
31	appropriate only after the potential of the previous parameter has been completely exploited. For example, it is 
32	unwise to increase training volume without having fully elicited the maximum training effect of the individual 
33	strength training means at a particular intensity. This requires dedication and persistence from the specialists, 
34	because it requires in-depth investigative effort Since increasing the training volume is easier than finding a really 
35	effective means of special preparation, such a course tends to be a much simpler choice.
36	4.2 Different Means of Strength Development
37	The external force generated by muscles is a result of voluntary effort. 
38	However, under normal everyday 
39	conditions, muscular tension produced by voluntary effort has certain limitations. 
40	To increase the external 
41	muscular force it is necessary to stimulate them from the outside, for example, by means of mechanical 
42	stimulation. Afferent impulses elicited by mechanical stimulation inform the central nervous system about the 
43	strength of the external influence evoking the muscular tension. The greater the intensity of the external stimulus, 
44	the greater the muscle effector discharge, and the larger the external work produced.
45	Thus, afferent signals to the neuromuscular system play an important role in determining the qualitative and 
46	quantitative characteristics of muscular strength. 
47	Therefore, the stimulation of muscular tension for the 
48	development of strength is of great significance. So, in all cases the magnitude of working muscular tension is 
49	determined by voluntary effort and external mechanical action. The stimulation of working force can be divided 
50	into the following basic types:
51	• Stimulation when muscular tension is produced by voluntary effort against external resistance, and the
52	resistance of the moving load accelerates and regulates the effector impulses to the muscles
53	• Stimulation by the kinetic energy of a falling object or the body, when the effort is primarily reflexive
54	• Stimulation caused primarily by voluntary effort, under conditions where additional external mechanical
55	stimulation is absent or limited
56	• Stimulation of muscle elicited or intensified involuntarily by means of external electrical current.
57	207
58	
59	
60	===== idx 219 / printed 208 =====
61	SUPERTRAINING
62	The first two cases are associated with dynamic work and the third with isometric work. 
63	An increase in 
64	stimulation is realised in the first case by increasing the velocity of the preliminary fall of the body or load, and by 
65	mobilising the athlete's voluntary resources in the third. It should also be pointed out that voluntary effort plays 
66	an important role in the magnitude of the effector response of the muscles in the first instance, whereas its 
67	influence in the second is insignificant.
68	The mechanism chiefly responsible for the braking or amortisation work of the muscles causes a protective 
69	effector response more rapidly than a voluntary sequence of actions. Therefore, such a reflex stimulus is able to 
70	provoke an extraordinary mobilisation of the neuromuscular apparatus, which is impossible where there is reliance 
71	on voluntary effort alone. This mechanism forms the foundation of plyometric training (5.2.4).
72	4.2.1 E lectrostim ulation
73	As has already been stated, there is always an ongoing search for novel, highly effective means of special strength 
74	training. For example, Russian studies have established that clcctrostimulation of muscle furnishes an adequate 
75	training stimulus for effective development of muscular strength (Kots, 1971; Kots & Khvilon, 1971; Khvilon, 
76	1974). Electrostimulation can be effective for certain purposes in the preparation of highly qualified athletes 
77	(mainly in speed-strength sports) and there are a number of advantages associated with this method of developing 
78	strength, in particular the reduction of joint loading. It can occupy a specific place in the yearly training cycle, be 
79	used in combination with other methods of developing muscular strength and be applied chiefly in the preparation 
80	of highly qualified athletes.
81	Ratov has found that functional electrical stimulation (FENS) can be particularly useful in improving sporting 
82	performance. His techniques, developed decades ago from his PhD programme on the interrelation between 
83	electrical stimulation and electromyography, has used EMG signals from agonist and antagonist muscles to act as 
84	triggers or control mechanisms for electrical stimulation of musclcs directly involved in producing functional 
85	movements in sport. In his laboratory at the State Central Institute for Sports Science in Moscow he has 
86	successfully implemented these neuromuscular stimulation methods in training athletes such as fencers, boxers, 
87	rowers, shotputtcrs and weightlifters.
88	However, it is inappropriate to consider the training applications of electrostimulation in detail here because 
89	its methodological fundamentals have still not been determined, especially as it should be applied preferably under 
90	suitable conditions by qualified personnel. 
91	The next section summarises the effects and applications of 
92	electrostimulation as a form of supplementary sports preparation.
93	4.2.1.1 The Physiological E ffects of Electrostim ulation
94	The concept o f elcctrostimulation is not new, and for years has been used by physical therapists in clinical 
95	applications such as muscle rehabilitation, relief of muscular spasm, reduction of swelling and pain control. Its 
96	possible value in sports training is still considered controversial. In strength conditioning, the applications of 
97	electrostimulation fall into the following broad categories:
98	• Imposition of local physical stress to provoke supercompensation
99	• Local restoration after exercise or injury
100	• General central nervous and endocrine restoration after exercise or injury
101	• Neuromuscular stimulation for pain control or movement patterning
102	Electrostimulation usually involves feeding the muscles low current electrical impulses via moistened electrode 
103	pads placed firmly on the skin. The effectiveness, comfort and depth of excitation depends on factors such as 
104	pulse shape, frequency, duration, intensity and modulation pattern. The resulting number of possible stimulation 
105	combinations immediately emphasizes how difficult it is to determine the optimum balance of variables and 
106	compare the results of different researchers.
107	The typical clinical machine supplies pulsating direct (galvanic) and/or alternating (faradic) current in the form 
108	of brief pulses. The frequency of faradic current is most commonly chosen in the range of about 50-100 Hz, while 
109	pulse duration (width) ranges from about 100 microseconds to several hundred milliseconds. This brevity of pulse 
110	duration is important to minimise skin irritation and tissue damage. However, the duration at any particular 
111	intensity of faradic stimulation should not be too brief Although they may be suitable for decreasing pain, pulses 
112	that are too brief will supply insufficient energy to cause full, tetanic muscle contraction.
113	208
114	
115	
116	===== idx 220 / printed 209 =====
117	SUPERTRAINING
118	Machines are designed to apply alternating currents directly at a preset or selected frequency (conventional 
119	faradism), or in the form of low frequency currents superimposed on a medium frequency (2000 to 5000 Hz) 
120	earner wave. A variation of the latter method, using two pairs of electrodes each supplying medium frequency 
121	waves carrying low frequency waves differing slightly in frequency, forms the basis of what is called interferential 
122	stimulation. A major advantage of using a higher frequency carrier wave is that impedance between the electrodes 
123	and skin is lowered, enhancing comfort and effectiveness.
124	American interest in electrostimuiation as a training adjunct was aroused in 1971, when Kots in Russia 
125	reported increases of more than 20% in muscle strength, speed and power produced by several weeks of 
126	dectrotraining. Unable to produce comparable results, the Canadians invited him to lecture at Concordia 
127	University in 1977. Armed with the new information that Kots employed a sinusoidally modulated 2500 Hz 
128	cunent source applied in a sequence of 10 seconds of contraction followed by 50 seconds of relaxation, they again 
129	tried to duplicate Russian claims.
130	It is noteworthy that this procedure differed significantly from that of top Belgian superheavy weightlifter. 
131	Serge Reding, who had close training contact with one of the authors (Siff) while he stayed with him In South 
132	Africa in the early 1970s. After training sessions he used 0.5 to 2 second, very high intensity contractions with 
133	10 to 15 second rest periods, for a total of 5 minutes per major muscic group, with agonists and antagonists of 
134	each limb alternately stimulated in ipsilateral and contralateral sequences (Siff, 1973). Reding always concluded 
135	his sessions with a few repetitions (1-3) of a long duration (10-15 seconds) fairly intense tetanic contraction to 
136	serve as a type o f deep massage, followed by about 10-15 minutes of microcurrent stimulation (less than 200 
137	microamps) applied across the head and spinal cord with another electrostimulator.
138	Despite the subsequent success reported by various track coaches in integrating conventional faradic 
139	electrostimulation into a carefully periodised training programme (Francis, 1982), researchers continue to disagree 
140	on increase in muscle strength.
141	4.2.1.2 Reasons for C onflicting Research
142	There are several main reasons for the contradictory research findings:
143	1. Many studies focus largely on isometric or isokinetic strength changes, which complicates research 
144	comparisons. Such research often neglects possible effects of other vital factors such as power, speed, muscular 
145	endurance, residual muscic tension, muscle growth and rate of neuromuscular recovery.
146	2. Much of the research examines injured patients in the process of rehabilitation, untrained individuals, or trained 
147	subjects from differing fitness and training backgrounds. 
148	It is well known that an increase in strength is 
149	proportionately greater in the early stages of a training programme or among untrained subjects. Moreover, 
150	increases in strength for novices during the first few weeks of training mainly are due to neuromuscular adaptation 
151	and learning, rather than muscle hypertrophy.
152	3. The effectiveness of electrostimuiation is determined by the intensity of the current used and individual 
153	tolerance of discomfort caused by stimulation. In addition, no specific waveform has been found to be universally 
154	most comfortable. There also can be considerable variation among subjects in their response to different 
155	waveforms and stimulation impedances (Delitto & Rose, 1986; Mannheimcr & Carlsson, 1979; Moreno-Aranda 
156	& Seirig, 1981).
157	4. The effects of electrostimuiation depend on the types and frequency of waveforms used, particularly since 
158	there is a distinct difference in the recruitment patterns and functional characteristics of slow-twitch and fast- 
159	twitch muscle fibres (Lloyd ct al, 1986; Mannheimer & Carlsson, 1979; Pette & Vrbova, 1985). Moreover, the 
160	higher the frequency, particularly if a carrier wave is used, the lower the impedance between electrodes and skin, 
161	and the greater the degree of comfort.
162	5. The type, size, number and location of electrodes, as well as the electrode gel, affect the amount of electrical 
163	energy transmitted to the muscles, the resultant force of contraction and patient comfort. Many studies do not 
164	discuss these details, and therefore, valid comparisons largely are meaningless.
165	6. Most studies have used commercial electrostimulators which arc able to vary only a few of all the possible 
166	stimulation parameters. Some of the more extensive studies have varied several of these parameters, as 
167	summarised in the thorough review by Lloyd et al (1986). However, because of the enormous number of
168	209
169	
170	
171	===== idx 221 / printed 210 =====
172	SUPERTRAINING
173	stimulation combinations theoretically possible, no single extensive study has been able to examine the effects of 
174	varying all the stimulation parameters. This includes frequency, waveform, pulse-width, type of modulation 
175	(Frequency Modulation, Amplitude Modulation or pulse-width modulation), impulse interval and electrical 
176	energy delivered.
177	7. The effects of electrostimulation, like plyometric training, may be enhanced by optimal integration into an 
178	overall strength and sport specific training programme (e.g. Francis, 1982)
179	8. Many of the training regimes have been deficiently designed. Usually, the electrostimulator is selected according 
180	to the maximum tolerated by subjects, or to a certain percentage of a maximal voluntary isometric or isokinetic 
181	contraction as measured on isokinetic or other dynamometers. It should be noted that adaptation to any stimulus 
182	occurs, and subjects can withstand greater intensities of electric current from the start to end of any session, and 
183	from week to week.
184	Similarly, studies examining the combined effects of electrostimulation and normal strength training often 
185	prescribe weight training with a fixed number of sets and loads at a fixed percentage of single repetition maximum, 
186	despite the fact that the latter maximum gradually increases. The accompanying electrical stimulation also is set at 
187	a fixed value, which fails to consider that the basic principle of strength and power enhancement is gradual 
188	overload. Such a training regime in normal weight training is known to be highly limited in improving physical 
189	performance. It would be surprising if it were any different with electrostimulation training.
190	9. The design and effects of the electrostimulator depend on the choice of physiological model. Most stimulators 
191	are designed on the basis of the action-potential model of nerve cell discharge, which considers that cellular 
192	communication in the body is mediated by bursts of electrical discharge transmitted along nerve axons. The cell is 
193	assumed to be W  (discharging electricity) or 'off (resting), depending on whether the build-up of electrical charge 
194	in the cell is large enough to exceed a certain threshold, rendering the cell membrane temporarily more permeable to 
195	certain chemical ions. Intermediate subthreshold states arc presumed unimportant, although they are central to an 
196	understanding of the EEG (brain waves) and other electrical potentials of the central nervous system (Siff, 1981).
197	Similarly, the numerous glial cells which surround all nerve cells are assumed to play little more than a 
198	nutritional or supportive role for the nerves, despite the fact that they display a steady or quasi-steady electric 
199	field (Galambos, 1961; Siff, 1981). Some scientists believe that glial cell potentials may have a profound effect on 
200	nerve cells by modulating their activity similar to semiconductors such as transistors in electronic circuits (Becker. 
201	1974; Galambos, 1961). In addition, the DC injury potentials measurable on the skin surface after tissue damage 
202	are not associated with the action potential system (Becker, 1982).
203	Moreover, little is known about electrical fields at the subcellular level. The sensitivity of the body to 
204	external electric, magnetic and electromagnetic fields cannot satisfactorily be explained in terms of action 
205	potentials, which are not directly affected by these fields (Becker, 1965; Cope, 1974). The classical theories also 
206	do not explain the mechanisms whereby electric and other fields stimulate processes such as the repair of 
207	fractures, the healing of wounds and reduction of thrombosis.
208	On discovering evidence for semiconduction and the possible existence of superconductivity at room 
209	temperature in biological systems, scientists now have postulated that tissue healing, pain mechanisms, cell 
210	growth and disease processes may involve biological semiconduction and superconductivity (Becker, 1965; Cope, 
211	1971; Cope, 1974). In addition, Nordenstrom claims to have shown the presence of closed electric circuits in the 
212	body, whereby ionic flow concerned with growth and regulatory processes takes place via blood vessels and 
213	through or along the capillaries (Nordenstrom, 1983).
214	All faradic, medium frequency and interferential stimulators (including sports-oriented machines) are designed 
215	on the action-potential model for cell operation, which, therefore, do not permit applications relying on the other 
216	types of models described above. Such applications involve cell growth, tissue repair and general recuperation, all 
217	of which are essential features of physical conditioning. In recent years a few innovative micro-current machines 
218	based on these models have been applied clinically with significant success in neuromuscular rehabilitation (Chee 
219	& Walton, 1986; Matteson, 1984; Matteson & Eberhardt, 185; Meyer & Nebrensky, 1983; Noto & Grant, 1985).
220	4.2.1.3 Clinical Applications of Electrostim ulation
221	At this point it is relevant to survey the clinical and research evidence supporting the value of elcctrostimulation 
222	in medical situations. Its major applications or effects are the following:
223	210
224	
225	
226	===== idx 222 / printed 211 =====
227	SUPERTRAINING
228	1. Increase in Muscle Strength
229	A wide range of low and medium frequencies has been shown to strengthen muscle tissue in the case of subjects 
230	who have been incapacitated by injury, illness or childbirth ( Eriksson, 1981; Johnson et al, 1977; Laughman et al, 
231	1983; Lloyd et al, 1986; Raitsin, 1974; Romero et al, 1982; Turk et al, 1980). Some studies on the effect of 
232	clectrostimulation (ES) alone on normal subjects also have revealed strength increases (Currier & Mann, 1983; 
233	Laughman et al, 1983: McMiken et al, 1983; Romero et al, 1982; Sekowitz, 1985), although some of these studies 
234	showed that ES was not superior to voluntary exercise (Currier & Mann, 1983; Laughmen et al, 1983; McMiken 
235	et al, 1983; Sckowitz, 1985). Further studies found minimal or insignificant changes in strength (Massey et al, 
236	1965; Mohr ct al, 1985; Singer etal, 1983).
237	In general, most of these studies indicate that ES unaccompanied by physical training at best produces long­
238	term strength gains which are similar to or smaller than those of voluntary exercise. The greatest strength increases 
239	are invariably found in the weakest or most unfit subjects (Fahey et al, 1985; Johnson et al, 1977; Romero et al, 
240	1982). However, in conjunction with periodised exercise programmes, ES appears to increase the strength of 
241	competitive athletes in some instances (Francis, 1982; Kots & Chwilon, 1971; Matteson, 1984; Reding, 1973), 
242	although these changes may have been the indirect result of some of the other effects of ES discussed below.
243	2. Re-education of Muscle Action
244	Some medical disorders or kinesiological habits may produce weak or faulty patterns of muscle action. ES may 
245	facilitate more efficient use of the affected muscles. It can be particularly effective in treating chondromalacia 
246	patellae, tennis elbow and 'frozen shoulder* (Eriksson, 1981; Godfrey et al, 1979; Johnson et al, 1977; Nirchl & 
247	Sobel, 1981).
248	3. Facilitation of Muscle Contraction
249	If one is unable to produce a voluntary muscle contraction because of disuse, pain or injury, ES can promote 
250	muscle activity and reduce the likelihood of extensive tissue wasting (Eriksson, 1981; Johnson ct al, 1977; Turk et
251	il, 1980; Vodovnik et al, 1982).
252	4. Increase of Muscular and Systemic Endurance
253	Prolonged application of sub-maximal ES can stimulate the fatiguing conditions encountered in strenuous physical 
254	work thereby increasing endurance o f the muscles involved (Ikai & Yabe, 1969; Johnson et al, 1977). Russian 
255	research reported improvement in cardiovascular efficiency, muscle contractility and rate of general recovery 
256	(Dombrovskaya, 1982). Moreover, low frequency (under 15 Hz) ES of long duration (24-hour) continuous 
257	stimulation experiments or cross-innervation experiments in animals have been shown to alter fast twitch fibres to 
258	bccome predominantly aerobic and more resistant to fatigue (Jolesz & Sreter, 1981; Pette, 1984; Pette & Vrbova, 
259	1985; Salmons & Vrbova, 1969; Salmons & Henriksson, 1981).
260	5. Increase of Speed of Muscle Contraction
261	Long-term higher frequency (more than 40 Hz) ES can improve reaction time and decrease the time to peak 
262	tension of fast twitch muscles (Fluery & Lagasse, 1979; Salmons & Vrbova, 1967, 1969).
263	6. Increase in Local Blood Supply
264	ES stimulates muscles to contract rhythmically, producing dilatation of the blood vessels, facilitating the transport 
265	of nutrients to the tissues, and possibly accelerating healing in tissues which are not extensively injured 
266	(Dombrovskaya, 1982; Salmons & Vrbova, 1967 Wadsworth & Chanmugam, 1980). Experiments using different

510	4.2.2 R esistance and Strength Training
511	In principle, the heavier the weight which muscles lift, the greater the tension they develop. The latter is achieved 
512	by the effective stimulation and recruitment into the work of a large proportion of the involved musclcs. Strength 
513	development through the use of resistance activity was demonstrated around 500 BC by the legendary Milo of 
514	Crotona. According to legend, he increased his strength enormously by lifting a young bull daily onto his 
515	shoulders. As the bull grew in mass, so did Milo's strength.
516	In our own era Milo's approach is exemplified by the DeLorme method o f progressive resistance exercise 
517	(DeLorme, 1945; DeLorme & Watkins, 1948, 1951). Essentially, this method consists of developing strength 
518	through repetitively lifting a weight which is gradually increased in the workout, as well from workout to 
519	workout, as strength increases.
520	However, when the display of great force was required, the imposition of resistance was a natural means of 
521	training, but where speed of movement plays a decisive role, resistance was used initially with great care. At the 
522	same time, some researchers noted that strength training makes it possible to improve results in speed type 
523	exercises (Dupperon, 1926; Lubimov, 1927; Curie, 1937; Markov, 1938, Ozolin, 1939; Chui, 1950; Gullwer, 
524	1955; Pennybaker, 1961). However, a long period of experimental and practical verification was required before 
525	this hypothesis gained acceptance. However, it is correct only relative to the amount of weight, the coordination 
526	pattern of the movement, the tempo and the number of repetitions.
527	When resistance is used for stimulating muscular tension, it is necessary to consider the fact that strength 
528	may be displayed in resistance exercises in the form of maximal tension or maximal speed of muscle contraction. 
529	One can then refer to strength exercises in which force is displayed primarily by increasing the amount of weight, 
530	and speed-strength exercises in which the display of force is associated with increasing the speed of movement 
531	(Farfel, 1940). In the first case, one tries to work with the largest resistance possible and in the second with a 
532	resistance whose optimal magnitude is determined by the required speed of movement.
533	It should be pointed out that the work regimes o f strength with primarily slow movements and speed- 
534	strength exercises (using inherently fast movements) are essentially different with respect to the physiological 
535	mechanisms and the manner in which energy resources are used. Execution of explosive movements invariably 
536	requires a high level of excitation of the basic neural processes. In the case of slow movements, the basic role of 
537	the nervous system is to produce sufficient excitation and maintain it for a relatively long period (Federov, 1957).
538	It is useful to examine more closely the dynamics of movements with maximal effort in terms of the 
539	magnitude of the resistance displaced and the regime of muscular work. The amount of work obviously increases 
540	as the load raised by a weightlifter is increased. However, the changes in the power output o f the work arc not 
541	unidirectional. Initially, power output increases, but after the weight of the barbell exceeds 66% of maximum, it 
542	begins to decrease (Chikvadze, 1961). A similar result is observed in the jump with a barbell on the shoulders (Fig 
543	4.2). Maximal dynamic force increases as the weight of the apparatus increases during the rapid increase in the 
544	movement time, mainly during the active thrust phase. Maximum power output is achieved with weights of 30- 
545	40% of the IRM and a maximal coefficient of reactivity at 30-33% of the 1RM.

589	to the distinctive effects associated with the torque produced by resistance exercises. For example, in the starting 
590	position for the squat and squat jumps (before beginning the dynamic effort), the muscles of the legs and torso 
591	have already developed tension equal to the weight of the apparatus being held. On the other hand, with the 
592	snatch or clean-and-jerk, the fundamental working force which accelerates the apparatus is developed practically

595	the apparatus)

598	influence the processes connected with physiological changes in the muscles (the cxcitation-tension link).

600	strength or the speed of muscular contraction, but not the speed with which muscles switch from rest to the

603	to understanding movement dynamics, but is very significant for improving strength training methods.

639	cadence, and opposing the angular momentum via eccentric muscle action to decelerate the wheel. One may 
640	combine all of these methods in short bursts or mixed bursts to offer a varied training regime.
641	Work with weights should be examined as a special case. Weights are used extensively for increasing the 
642	difficulty of movement to develop various motor abilities. Elastic bands are also frequently used as a means of 
643	resisting movement, although the character o f the force produced depends upon the elastic properties of the 
644	material, which limits the effectiveness of these means. Elastic force occurs in accordance with Hooke's Law: F = 
645	Lx, where k is the spring constant and x is the extension. Thus, elastic force increases with degree of extension, so 
646	that resistance begins from zero value and increases with movement range. Therefore, elastic materials should not 
647	be used for developing starting-strength in ballistic movements or for developing explosive-strength.

657	tension is proportional to extension, according to Hooke’s Law). Resistance can be varied over the full range of 
658	movement by accelerating free weights when resistance is decreasing (so-called “Compensatory Acceleration 
659	Training’) or by using special varying resistance machines, and this method of altering elastic length by postural 
660	idjustment also allows one to use elastics to optimise resistance, if required.
661	The methods of resisted movement are extremely diverse. In each case they are determined by the exercise 
662	and the resolution of two tasks: stimulation of muscular contraction and facilitation of transfer to the natural 
663	conditions of the movement (for example, putting a regulation shot after training with an overweight one). 
664	Movements can be made more difficult with small weights, thereby insignificantly increasing the mass of the body 
665	or its links. This may be accomplished with belts, weights, cuffs, sandbags, boots and other apparatus.

673	developing speed of 
674	movement (e.g. using the speed of unloaded movement or movement against a relatively small external resistance),
