14	# The Authors' MACS/MICS Theory of Electrostimulation: A Speculative Synthesis, Not a Settled Mechanism
15	
16	**What it is** — Building on research showing that very low currents (as little as 10
17	microamps, far below the milliamp-range currents of standard faradic/TENS devices) can
18	match or exceed conventional electrostimulation's (ES) benefits without causing contraction,
19	pain blockade or heating (Matteson & Eberhardt, 1985), the authors propose an "integrated
20	theory": macroelectric cellular stimulation (**MACS**, currents exceeding one milliamp) acts
21	as a physiological stressor producing Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome-type alarm
22	response (citing Eriksson et al, 1981, who found traditional ES's acute effects resemble
23	intense voluntary exercise; and Gambke et al, 1985, who found in animal studies that
24	long-term MACS causes some, mainly fast-twitch, fibres to degenerate and be replaced via
25	satellite-cell proliferation). Applying Selye's model (see 1.16), the body would draw on
26	"superficial adaptation energy stores" to adapt to MACS via increased strength, endurance,
27	or fibre-type transformation; if the ES is too intense, prolonged or misapplied, adaptation
28	might fail or shift toward slow-twitch fibres and reduced strength, and "excessively
29	demanding MACS conceivably might cause the body to draw on its deep adaptation energy and
30	lead to permanent tissue damage." Microelectric cellular stimulation (**MICS**, currents
31	below one milliamp) is proposed not to act as a stressor at all, but to elicit biochemical
32	changes tied to "resonant attunement" of the stimulus to cellular/subcellular processes,
33	citing a chain of supporting findings: Becker and colleagues on sub-threshold modulation of
34	electric fields across nerve and glial cells regulating growth and communication, including
35	wound-healing acceleration and partial limb regeneration in animals (Becker, 1974; Becker &
36	Marino, 1982); Nordenstrom's proposed "closed electric circuits" in the body carrying ionic
37	flow via blood vessels (Nordenstrom, 1983); Pilla's (1974) electrochemical membrane-signaling
38	model and "cellular windows" that respond most to specific frequencies, pulse widths and
39	amplitudes (Pilla, 1981); Rodan et al (1978), who found 5 Hz ES stimulated DNA synthesis in
40	chick cartilage and rat bone by up to 27% (but not in chick skin fibroblasts or rat spleen
41	lymphocytes) 4-6 hours after 15 minutes of stimulation; and Cheng et al (1982), who found
42	50-1000 microamp currents increased rat tissue ATP concentration by 300-500% and amino-acid
43	transport/protein synthesis by up to 40%, while currents above one milliamp depressed ATP
44	and protein synthesis (traditional ES commonly exceeds 20 milliamps, at which point this
45	depression is "nearly 50%"). Practical implication drawn from the theory: MICS can be used
46	far more routinely than MACS, since it "cannot produce overtraining or injury," while MACS
47	should be dosed and progressed like any other training stressor. (PDF pp. 224-227, printed
48	pp. 213-216, "4.2.1.4 Further Research Findings" and "4.2.1.5 An Integrated Theory of
49	Electrostimulation.")
50	
51	**Why it works** — This is the authors' own proposed synthesis, not a mechanism independently
52	established elsewhere in the text. It rests on two distinct evidentiary threads of very
53	different standing: (a) a defensible, mainstream physiological point that MACS-range ES acts
54	as a training/adaptation stressor subject to a dose-response and overtraining risk (the
55	Selye/Eriksson/Gambke citations); and (b) a set of bioelectromagnetic claims (Becker's
56	regeneration work, Nordenstrom's "biologically closed electric circuits," Pilla's cellular
57	windows) that were speculative even by 1990s standards and have not entered mainstream
58	sports-science or clinical practice as the general theory of cell communication the authors
59	present them as. The authors themselves flag some of this as still-developing: "little is
60	known about electrical fields at the subcellular level," and classical action-potential
61	theory "does not explain the mechanisms whereby electric and other fields stimulate
62	processes such as the repair of fractures... and reduction of thrombosis" (printed 210).
63	
64	**When to apply** — Inference: the (a) thread, that macro-current ES functions as a
65	stressor requiring progressive dosing rather than a fixed protocol, is a reasonable,
66	generally-applicable caution consistent with basic training-load principles and does not
67	depend on accepting thread (b). Do not use this entry to justify low-current "microcurrent"
68	devices for performance claims (tissue repair beyond standard wound-healing use, cellular
69	"resonance," or Nordenstrom-style circuit theory) without independent, modern verification
70	outside this book.
71	
72	**When NOT to apply** — Marked contested: several supporting claims in thread (b) (glial-cell
73	signaling as a major regulatory pathway comparable to semiconductor circuits; Nordenstrom's
74	"closed electric circuits"; "resonant attunement" as the operative principle of MICS) are
75	not mainstream, independently-replicated physiology as of this ingest, and this entry does
76	not attempt to verify them against current literature. The Rodan (1978) and Cheng (1982)
77	findings are animal/cell-culture studies (chick cartilage, rat bone, rat tissue) at specific
78	narrow current ranges; they do not establish that MICS produces the general "growth,
79	adaptation and repair" effects the authors attribute to it in human athletes. Do not treat
80	"MACS" and "MICS" as terms used outside this text; they appear to be the authors' own
81	coinage for this section.
82	
83	**Example** — Inference: a practitioner who reads "10-microamp microcurrent devices are as
84	effective as faradic stimulators without the risks" should recognize this claim rests
85	primarily on thread (b) above (Becker, Nordenstrom, Pilla), not on independently replicated
86	modern evidence, and should treat performance or healing claims for such devices with the
87	same skepticism the authors themselves apply to unverified action-potential-only models.
88	
89	**Related** — [[framework--clinical-physiological-effects-of-electrostimulation]],
90	[[heuristic--electrostimulation-sequencing-dosage-and-safety-practicalities]] (the
91	practical dosing limits the authors draw partly from this theory).
92

14	# Practical Rules for Integrating Electrostimulation Into a Programme: Sequencing, Electrode Placement, Dose Limits
15	
16	**What it is** — Several Russian researchers (Purvin, Deniskin, Khodykin, cited without
17	individual dates) studied how electrostimulation (ES) combines with other training means and
18	found that using ES first, followed by plyometrics, produces a greater training effect than
19	the reverse order; a still larger effect came from using ES and plyometrics concurrently
20	with heavy resistance exercise, while the ES-plyometric combination had its smallest
21	training effect during periods of complete or partial rest. Electrode placement matters:
22	adjacent (close) electrode attachment localises the contraction and keeps it fairly
23	superficial, while distant attachment (one electrode placed at a remote or neutral site)
24	produces a more extensive, deeper contraction; electrode gel or weak saline solution is
25	needed for comfortable conduction, and skin irritation or prickliness "invariably" results
26	from the gel drying out. Placing electrodes directly over major nerves increases contraction
27	intensity but "can be harmful," and the authors restrict this to use by experienced physical
28	therapists. On dosing: it is "generally not advisable to apply more than 5-10 minutes of
29	intense ES per major muscle group," due to associated tissue necrosis and prolonged soreness
30	that can follow (see [[claim--macs-mics-integrated-theory-of-electrostimulation]] for the
31	macroelectric/microelectric distinction behind this limit); biofeedback TENS devices that
32	monitor cellular electrical characteristics and adjust parameters automatically reduce
33	overstimulation risk. The authors' closing recommendation is that "the untutored reader is
34	not encouraged to use ES," since safe, effective application "requires considerable
35	theoretical and practical training," and that casual users typically see only sporadic,
36	short-term progress before discontinuing within a few months; in several countries
37	(the authors name the USA), ES devices may not legally be sold to the public or used
38	commercially by anyone without medical or physiotherapy training. (PDF pp. 225-227, printed
39	pp. 214-216, "4.2.1.6 The Use of Electrostimulation in Training.")
40	
41	**Why it works** — For the sequencing finding, the authors give no separate mechanism here
42	beyond the general after-effect logic already stated for training order (see
43	[[framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order]]): ES applied first may
44	potentiate the neuromuscular state for the plyometric work that follows, and the combined
45	concurrent condition with heavy resistance stacks all three stimuli within the same session
46	window. For electrode placement, the mechanism is straightforwardly the current's path
47	through tissue between the two electrode sites. For the dose limit, the mechanism given
48	(tissue necrosis, prolonged soreness) implies macro-current ES imposes real mechanical/metabolic
49	stress on the stimulated tissue, consistent with the MACS-as-stressor framing.
50	
51	**When to apply** — Use the sequencing finding (ES before plyometrics beats the reverse; ES
52	plus plyometrics concurrent with heavy resistance beats either combination alone) as a
53	specific instance of the book's broader non-commutative-training-order argument (see
54	[[framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order]]) when programming ES within a
55	session. Use the 5-10 minute per-muscle-group ceiling and the electrode-placement guidance
56	as baseline practical limits if ES is added to a programme, and restrict direct-over-nerve
57	placement to trained personnel.
58	
59	**When NOT to apply** — The sequencing citations (Purvin, Deniskin, Khodykin) give no dates,
60	sample sizes, or effect-size numbers in this passage, only a directional ranking of four
61	conditions (ES-then-plyometrics; plyometrics-then-ES; ES+plyometrics+heavy resistance
62	concurrent; ES+plyometrics during rest); treat this as a single-lab directional finding, not
63	a quantified prescription. The authors' own recommendation against untutored use, and the
64	legal restrictions they cite, mean this entry should not be read as a self-administration
65	guide; it summarises the book's own cautions, not a certified protocol.
66	
67	**Example** — Inference: a strength coach considering adding ES to a plyometric-heavy block
68	should schedule the ES stimulus before the plyometric work in the same session (per the
69	cited ranking), keep any single muscle group's intense ES exposure under 10 minutes, and use
70	adjacent electrode placement for a more localised, superficial target versus distant
71	placement for a deeper, more extensive contraction.
72

74	[[claim--macs-mics-integrated-theory-of-electrostimulation]],
75	[[framework--clinical-physiological-effects-of-electrostimulation]].

14	# Muscle Recruitment Stays Fairly Consistent at Moderate Loads but Shifts Toward Proximal Muscles as Resistance or Velocity Rises
15	
16	**What it is** — Two related findings on how muscle involvement changes with load and
17	velocity during repetitive barbell lifting. First, the "most stable indicator" of
18	coordinated muscular activity in repetitive lifting is the sequential involvement of the
19	same specific muscles across reps: in an experiment at 60% of 1RM, the muscles taking part
20	in the work remained the same for 82% of the time across all athletes tested; at 80% of
21	1RM, consistency was lower (showing greater individuality), but higher among qualified
22	athletes than novices, and fatigue also disrupted coordination (Pakhomov, 1967). The
23	relative contribution of participating muscles can also change during repetitive work
24	(Lazareva, 1966; Kozlov, 1966), and the number of muscle groups involved can either decrease
25	(Moikin, 1964) or increase (Averyanov, 1963) as a set progresses. Second, movements executed
26	with little effort or low velocity involve mostly the muscles of the body's distal links
27	(Tochilov, 1946; Kosilov, 1948; Vinogradov, 1951); against significant resistance or at high
28	velocity, activity characteristically shifts to the muscles of the proximal links, "which
29	tend to play a more tonic or postural role." The authors draw a direct implication from this
30	second finding: "muscle isolation under conditions of significant resistance is impossible,"
31	a point developed later in the chapter (see
32	[[claim--muscle-isolation-is-load-dependent-mostly-illusory-under-heavy-load]]). (PDF p.
33	229, printed p. 218, "4.2.2 Resistance and Strength Training.")

35	**Why it works** — No explicit mechanism is given for why recruitment consistency at 60% of
36	1RM (82%) exceeds that at 80% of 1RM, only the observation that qualified athletes show
37	greater consistency than less qualified ones at the higher load, and that fatigue disrupts
38	it further. Inference: this is consistent with the general principle that skilled athletes
39	have more stable, better-rehearsed motor patterns, which higher loads and fatigue both stress
40	more than lower loads. For the proximal/distal shift, the authors give no mechanism beyond
41	the empirical citations; Inference: this is plausibly related to proximal muscles' larger
42	cross-sectional area and postural/stabilising role becoming more necessary as the system
43	must resist larger external forces or move faster.
44

46	when interpreting EMG or force-plate data collected across a set: consistency of which
47	muscles are active can itself change with load and fatigue state, independent of the
48	athlete's technique intent. Use the proximal/distal shift finding when auditing exercise
49	selection for "isolation" claims at high resistance: expect proximal, postural muscle
50	involvement to increase, not stay constant, as load or velocity rises. **Eric's baseline:**
51	this is directly relevant to interpreting force-plate strategy metrics (phase durations,
52	which segments contribute) that vary with load, per the department's driver/strategy metric

17	inertia (rather than its weight) is rarely used, despite the concept warranting more serious

19	suspended, pendulum-like load, or spinning a heavy flywheel ergometer with the arms or legs
20	(Fig 4.4, elbow-flexion flywheel device, Verkhoshansky 1977). A flywheel device's moment of
21	inertia can be varied to change the speed-of-contraction demand, and it can be used several
22	ways: accelerating against high inertia, using the wheel's momentum to compel a certain
23	movement cadence, or opposing the wheel's angular momentum via eccentric muscle action to
24	decelerate it, with these methods combinable in short or mixed bursts. Elastic bands are
25	treated as a separate special case: resistance follows Hooke's Law (F = kx, where k is the
26	spring constant and x is extension), so elastic force starts at zero and rises with range of
27	movement; the authors state plainly that "elastic materials should not be used for
28	developing starting-strength in ballistic movements or for developing explosive-strength,"
29	because those qualities need force available from the very start of the movement, which
30	elastics cannot supply. For strength-endurance over a selected range, however, an elastic
31	band's length and elasticity can be chosen so its resistance changes minimally over the
32	working range, a method used by swimmers to develop pulling strength-endurance (Fig 4.5,
33	Verkhoshansky 1977). Resistance at "sticking points" can be reduced by moving toward the
34	band's attachment point, or increased by moving away from it; resistance can also be varied
35	across the full range by accelerating free weights through a decreasing-resistance portion
36	of the lift (so-called Compensatory Acceleration Training, see
37	[[framework--compensatory-acceleration-training]]) or by using dedicated variable-resistance
38	machines. (PDF pp. 219-220, printed pp. 219-220, "4.2.2 Resistance and Strength Training,"

43	athlete can train speed of contraction against a resistance that does not exist at rest, only
44	once acceleration is applied, unlike a gravity-loaded free weight. For elastic bands, the

47	curve from what ballistic and explosive-strength work typically needs (high force available

# Four Ways to Stimulate Working Muscular Tension, and How They Map to the Rest of the Chapter

**What it is** — External muscular force is a product of voluntary effort, but voluntary
effort alone has limits; the authors classify how "stimulation of working force" is
supplied from outside that voluntary effort into four basic types: (1) muscular tension
produced by voluntary effort against external resistance, where the moving load's
resistance "accelerates and regulates the effector impulses to the muscles"; (2)
stimulation by the kinetic energy of a falling object or the body, where "the effort is
primarily reflexive"; (3) stimulation caused primarily by voluntary effort under conditions
where additional external mechanical stimulation is absent or limited; and (4) stimulation
of muscle "elicited or intensified involuntarily by means of external electrical current."
The authors group the first two as dynamic work and the third as isometric work; for the
first, increased stimulation comes from increasing the velocity of the preliminary fall of
the body or load; for the third, from "mobilising the athlete's voluntary resources."
Voluntary effort plays an important role in the first case, but is "insignificant" in the
second (the falling-body case), where the braking/amortisation mechanism produces a
protective reflex response faster than a voluntary sequence of actions can. This forms the
basis of plyometric training (see [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]]).
This four-way classification sets up the rest of the chapter's structure: type (4) is
covered next as 4.2.1 Electrostimulation, type (1) as 4.2.2 Resistance and Strength
Training, type (2) as 4.2.3 Kinetic Energy and Strength Processes, and type (3) as 4.2.4
Isometric Training. (PDF p. 218, printed p. 207, "4.2 Different Means of Strength
Development.")

**Why it works** — The authors' stated reason: afferent impulses elicited by mechanical
stimulation inform the central nervous system about the strength of the external
influence evoking muscular tension, and "the greater the intensity of the external
stimulus, the greater the muscle effector discharge, and the larger the external work
produced." Inference: this is a general afferent-feedback framing rather than a
mechanism specific to any one of the four types; the chapter's later sections give more
detailed, type-specific mechanisms (e.g. elastic energy storage for the falling-body case,
gradual overload for the resistance case).

**When to apply** — Use this as an organizing checklist when auditing a program's strength
means: does a given exercise stimulate tension primarily through external resistance,
through absorbed kinetic energy (a fall or catch), through sustained voluntary effort with
little external aid (isometric), or through externally applied electrical current? Mixing
means from more than one category (e.g. resistance plus electrostimulation) is a distinct
programming decision from staying within one category, and the chapter's later sections
(4.2.1 Electrostimulation, "Sports Functional Electrostimulation") discuss combining
categories explicitly.

**When NOT to apply** — Inference: this is the book's own convenience classification for
organizing chapter 4.2, not a claim that these four mechanisms are mutually exclusive
within a single exercise (a depth jump followed by a jump, for example, combines kinetic-
energy stimulation with subsequent voluntary resistance work). Do not treat the four-way
split as a measurement protocol; it carries no associated testing method here.

**Example** — Inference: a coach comparing a paused back squat (voluntary effort against
external resistance, type 1), a depth jump (kinetic energy of a fall, type 2), a wall sit
(sustained voluntary isometric effort, type 3), and a quadriceps NMES session (external
electrical current, type 4) is comparing four different stimulation mechanisms for the same
target muscle group, each covered by a different subsection of this chapter. This example
is not in the source.

**Related** — [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]] (Ch1, the falling-body
mechanism this framework's type 2 builds on); [[framework--precise-muscle-action-terminology]]
(Ch1, the mechanical regimes -concentric, eccentric, isometric- this framework's types map
onto at the muscle-action level, a distinct but adjacent classification).

52:- Stretching and electrostimulation did not significantly improve DOMS or fatigue in the pooled analyses. [p. 11]
56:- Publication and English/French language restriction bias may have inflated effects. [p. 11]
57:- Substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity remained, and the interaction between the preceding training load and modality effectiveness could not be resolved. [p. 11]

59:- Performance recovery was not evaluated, repeated use and combined modalities were excluded, and changes in soreness or biomarkers should not be assumed to equal restored performance. [pp. 11-12]

# Peak Power Load Is Very Different in the Lab (~25% Max) vs a Real Competition Lift (~65-70% Max)

**What it is** — In simple isotonic muscle-contraction models, power (P = F x V) peaks at
roughly one-third of maximal contraction speed and one-quarter of maximal force: that is,
maximal isotonic power is displayed against a load requiring about 25% of the muscle's
maximal force (Wilkie, 1950). But the text explicitly warns this laboratory pattern "can
differ significantly" from functional, multi-joint activities: in the competitive
powerlifting squat, peak power for a group of elite (+125 kg class) lifters (mean best
squat 407.4 kg) occurred at a load of about **280 kg, roughly two-thirds of their maximum**,
producing 1451 watts over 0.85 seconds; power dropped to 52% of that peak at maximal load,
and time to execute the lift "increases by 282%" (the text does not state the reference
point this percentage is measured from). (PDF pp. 157-158, printed pp. 146-147, "3.3.2 The
Effect of the Load on Speed of Muscle Contraction," Fig 3.17.)

**Why it works** — The text gives no mechanism beyond noting the mismatch between
idealized single-muscle isotonic models and the real biomechanics of a multi-joint,
whole-body competition lift. **Inference:** a full competition squat recruits many muscle
groups and joints with different individual force-velocity properties, technique
constraints, and stability demands that a single-muscle isotonic model cannot capture,
which could explain why the practical power-peak load sits well above the single-muscle
theoretical prediction, but the book itself does not offer this or any other explanation.

**When to apply** — Use the ~65-70%-of-1RM figure, not the classical 25%-of-max figure,
when programming loads intended to maximize power output in barbell squat-pattern lifts

# Case Study: Siff's Account of Serge Reding's Electrostimulation Protocol

**What it is** — The authors describe (p.209, third person) Serge Reding, the top Belgian
superheavyweight weightlifter, "who had close training contact with one of the authors
(Siff) while he stayed with him in South Africa in the early 1970s" (citing Siff, 1973). On
p.215 Siff writes of "the ES training applied to the author by Serge Reding". Reding's
post-session electrostimulation (ES) protocol differed significantly from Kots's (see
[[claim--kots-electrostimulation-strength-claims-not-replicated]]): after training sessions
he used 0.5 to 2 second, very high intensity contractions with 10 to 15 second rest
periods, for a total of 5 minutes per major muscle group, "with agonists and antagonists of
each limb alternately stimulated in ipsilateral and contralateral sequences" (p.209). Reding
always concluded his sessions with a few repetitions (1-3) of a long-duration (10-15 second),
fairly intense tetanic contraction to serve as a type of deep massage, followed by about
10-15 minutes of microcurrent stimulation (less than 200 microamps) applied across the head
and spinal cord with another electrostimulator (p.209). On p.215 the stimulator is named as a
Myogen Parametric stimulator "designed to offer external stimulation which in no way
simulated the most frequently occurring movements of Olympic lifting", so that ES served as
a form of General Physical Preparation (GPP). "The intensity of the ES was carefully
periodised into the entire training programme alongside other key methods of strength
training", and sessions "were always terminated with brief, deep ES muscle massage and
restorative microstimulation across the brain and along the length of the spinal cord"
(p.215). Reding "stressed the importance of different waveforms and regimes of FES for
different categories of sport, adding that the method shared by Kots with Canadian coaches
was only one of many possibilities" (p.215).

The book describes the stimulation pattern two ways. p.209: agonists and antagonists of each
limb alternately stimulated, ipsilateral and contralateral. p.215: "The Reding machine
applied brief intense pulses alternately in a flip-flop fashion to opposite sides of the
body, though not to paired agonists and antagonists." Both are recorded; the book does not
reconcile them. (PDF p. 220, printed p. 209, "4.2.1.1"; PDF p. 226, printed p. 215, "4.2.1.6
The Use of Electrostimulation in Training.")

**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism for why this dosing pattern (brief,
high-intensity contractions; alternating stimulation; a closing deep-massage-style tetanic
contraction; low-current cranial-spinal microstimulation) would produce a training effect.
The passage is a descriptive account of practice, not an experiment.

**When to apply** — Inference: use this as a documented example that elite-level ES
protocols in this era varied substantially among people using the same broad technology; it
is not evidence that Reding's protocol outperformed Kots's, only that it existed and was
applied to a top-level athlete, with Siff as the subject (p.215).

**When NOT to apply** — Untested: this is a single account, received by Siff as the subject
(p.215) and described from Reding's own practice (p.209), with no reported outcome data (no
before/after strength numbers), no control condition, and no independent replication in the
text. The book's own two descriptions of the stimulation pattern disagree (see above). Do not
treat the specific timings (0.5-2 s contractions, 10-15 s rest, 5 min per muscle group,
10-15 min microcurrent under 200 microamps, p.209) as a validated prescription.

**Example** — The book's own example is this case itself: Reding's protocol, received by
Siff as the subject (p.215) and described from Reding's own practice (p.209). No further
example is added here.

**Related** — [[claim--kots-electrostimulation-strength-claims-not-replicated]],
[[claim--ratov-functional-electrostimulation-emg-triggered-sport-specific]] (a different,
contemporaneous Soviet approach that Siff also witnessed).

# Kots's 20%+ Electrostimulation Strength Claims Aroused American Interest; the Book Reports Failed Canadian Duplication and Continuing Disagreement

**What it is** — "American interest in electrostimulation as a training adjunct was aroused
in 1971, when Kots in Russia reported increases of more than 20% in muscle strength, speed
and power produced by several weeks of electrotraining." The Canadians could not first
produce comparable results: "Unable to produce comparable results, the Canadians invited him
to lecture at Concordia University in 1977." Armed with the information that Kots employed a
sinusoidally modulated 2500 Hz current source applied in a sequence of 10 seconds of
contraction followed by 50 seconds of relaxation, "they again tried to duplicate Russian
claims." The book does not report that outcome (PDF p. 220, printed p. 209). It gives no rep
or set count for Kots's protocol.

The same section states both sides of the strength question. Russian studies "have
established that electrostimulation of muscle furnishes an adequate training stimulus for
effective development of muscular strength (Kots, 1971; Kots & Khvilon, 1971; Khvilon,
1974)" (PDF p. 219, printed p. 208). Yet, despite the success various track coaches reported
in integrating conventional faradic ES into a carefully periodised programme (Francis, 1982),
"researchers continue to disagree on increase in muscle strength" (PDF p. 220, printed
p. 209). The clinical-effects list also names Kots & Chwilon (1971) among the sources for ES
appearing "to increase the strength of competitive athletes in some instances" with
periodised exercise (PDF p. 222, printed p. 211). `contested` is set for this internal
disagreement. (PDF pp. 219-220, printed pp. 208-209, "4.2.1 Electrostimulation" and
"4.2.1.1 The Physiological Effects of Electrostimulation.")

**Why it works** — The authors give no physiological mechanism for why Kots's protocol
(2500 Hz, 10 s on, 50 s off) would or would not replicate. The later "Reasons for
Conflicting Research" subsection (see
[[heuristic--nine-reasons-electrostimulation-research-conflicts]]) gives general
methodological reasons ES research disagrees, without resolving the Kots case.

**When to apply** — Inference: treat any single large ES strength-gain percentage (here,
"more than 20%") as a claim tied to one fully specified protocol (waveform, frequency, duty
cycle) from one lab, not a property of "electrostimulation" as a category. The Canadians
could not first produce comparable results; after obtaining Kots's parameters they "again
tried to duplicate" the claims, and the book does not report that outcome (p.209).
Inference: the book's account therefore does not show the claims were replicated.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a single historical claim and one reported duplication
effort from the 1970s, with no outcome given and no independent modern confirmation in this
text. Do not cite "more than 20%" as an expected or typical ES strength gain. Do not cite the
book as showing that the claims were replicated or refuted: it states both "have
established" (p.208) and "continue to disagree" (p.209).

**Example** — Inference: a strength coach weighing NMES for a rehabilitating athlete should
ask what waveform, frequency and duty cycle a cited study used. The page gives three facts
for Kots's case: the Canadians could not produce comparable results, invited Kots to
Concordia in 1977, and, armed with his parameters, tried again; the outcome is not reported
(p.209).

**Related** — [[heuristic--nine-reasons-electrostimulation-research-conflicts]],
[[case-study--reding-electrostimulation-protocol-siff-account]] (a contemporaneous,
differently designed elite-athlete ES protocol the authors set against the Kots/Canadian
history), [[claim--strength-detraining-and-retention-timelines]] (Khvilon 1974 ES strength
retention).

# Kots's 20%+ Electrostimulation Strength Claims Drew Western Interest but Were Not Replicated

**What it is** — American interest in electrostimulation (ES) as a training adjunct was
aroused in 1971, when Kots in Russia reported increases of more than 20% in muscle
strength, speed and power produced by several weeks of "electrotraining." Unable to
produce comparable results, Canadian researchers invited Kots to lecture at Concordia
University in 1977; armed with the detail that Kots used a sinusoidally modulated 2500 Hz
current source applied in a sequence of 10 seconds of contraction followed by 50 seconds of
relaxation, they again tried to duplicate the Russian claims. The authors report that "researchers
continue to disagree on increase in muscle strength" despite this, and separately note that
various track coaches reported success integrating conventional faradic ES into a
carefully periodised training programme (Francis, 1982). (PDF pp. 219-220, printed pp.
208-209, "4.2.1.1 The Physiological Effects of Electrostimulation.")

**Why it works** — The authors give no physiological mechanism for why Kots's specific
protocol (2500 Hz carrier, 10s on/50s off) would or would not replicate; the chapter's
later "Reasons for Conflicting Research" subsection (see
[[heuristic--nine-reasons-electrostimulation-research-conflicts]]) gives the general
methodological reasons ES research disagrees, without resolving the Kots case specifically.

**When to apply** — Inference: treat any single large ES strength-gain percentage (here,
"more than 20%") as a claim tied to one specific, fully-specified protocol (waveform,
frequency, duty cycle) from one lab, not a generic property of "electrostimulation" as a
category; the Canadian replication attempt failed using a different protocol until they
obtained Kots's exact parameters, and even then the authors do not report the Canadian
outcome as a confirmed success.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a single historical claim and a single replication attempt,
both from the 1970s, without independent modern confirmation in this text. Do not cite "20%
plus" as an expected or typical ES strength gain; the chapter itself frames Kots's number as
contested rather than settled, and the following subsection lists nine separate
methodological reasons why ES strength research across studies disagrees.

**Example** — Inference: a strength coach considering NMES for a rehabilitating athlete
should ask what specific waveform, frequency and duty cycle any cited study used, since this
entry shows that even a direct attempt to replicate one well-specified protocol required
obtaining that protocol's exact parameters from its originator before a comparable attempt
could be made.

[[case-study--reding-electrostimulation-protocol-siff-account]] (a contemporaneous but
differently-designed elite-athlete ES protocol the authors set against the Kots/Canadian

# Nine Reasons Electrostimulation Strength Research Disagrees: A Checklist for Reading It

**What it is** — The authors give nine specific methodological reasons why published
electrostimulation (ES) strength-training studies contradict one another: (1) many studies
measure only isometric or isokinetic strength change and neglect power, speed, muscular
endurance, residual muscle tension, muscle growth and rate of neuromuscular recovery; (2)
much research uses injured or rehabilitating patients, untrained individuals, or trained
subjects of differing backgrounds, and strength gains are proportionately larger early in
training or in untrained subjects, with early gains driven mainly by neuromuscular
adaptation and learning rather than hypertrophy; (3) ES effectiveness depends on current
intensity and individual tolerance of discomfort, and no waveform has been found to be
universally most comfortable, with considerable inter-subject variation (Delitto & Rose,
1986; Mannheimer & Carlsson, 1979; Moreno-Aranda & Seirig, 1981); (4) effects depend on
waveform type and frequency, since slow-twitch and fast-twitch fibres have distinct
recruitment patterns and functional characteristics (Lloyd et al, 1986; Mannheimer &
Carlsson, 1979; Pette & Vrbova, 1985), and higher frequency (especially with a carrier
wave) lowers electrode-skin impedance and raises comfort; (5) electrode type, size, number,
location and gel affect delivered energy, resultant contraction force and comfort, and many
studies omit these details, "so valid comparisons largely are meaningless"; (6) most
studies use commercial stimulators that vary only a few of the many possible stimulation
parameters (frequency, waveform, pulse-width, modulation type, impulse interval, energy
delivered), so no single study has examined the full parameter space, even in the more
extensive review by Lloyd et al (1986); (7) ES effects, like plyometric training, may be
enhanced or diminished by how well it is integrated into an overall strength and
sport-specific programme (e.g. Francis, 1982); (8) many training regimes are deficiently
designed, setting ES intensity at a fixed value (or a fixed percentage of maximal voluntary
isometric/isokinetic contraction) that does not progress as the subject adapts, the same
flaw that limits fixed-load weight training; (9) the design and effects of a stimulator
depend on which physiological model of cellular communication it assumes (the
action-potential model versus subthreshold/bioelectric models), a design choice most
commercial stimulators do not make explicit (see
[[claim--macs-mics-integrated-theory-of-electrostimulation]]). (PDF pp. 220-221, printed pp.
209-210, "4.2.1.2 Reasons for Conflicting Research.")

**Why it works** — The authors' own framing: these are methodological confounds (measurement
scope, subject population, dosing, hardware specification, and underlying physiological
model), not evidence for or against ES itself; a study that controls for none of these nine
factors cannot be meaningfully compared with one that controls for a different subset.

**When to apply** — Use this as a checklist before citing any single ES strength-training
study: what outcome was measured (item 1), who were the subjects (item 2), was the current
intensity and waveform reported and justified (items 3-4, 6), were electrode details given
(item 5), was the training programme context described (item 7), and did the dosing
progress with adaptation (item 8)? A study missing several of these items should be treated
as weak evidence regardless of its stated conclusion.

**When NOT to apply** — Inference: this checklist evaluates methodological rigor, not
whether ES "works"; a study can satisfy all nine points and still report a negative or null
result, and the authors elsewhere report both positive and negative ES findings that passed
some of these criteria (see
[[framework--clinical-physiological-effects-of-electrostimulation]]). Do not use this list
to dismiss all ES research wholesale; use it to weight individual studies.

**Example** — Inference: a marketing claim citing "a study showing 20% strength gains from
electrostimulation" should be checked against this list: was the outcome purely isometric
(item 1)? Were the subjects untrained or rehabilitating (item 2)? Was the current intensity
fixed for the whole programme (item 8)? Failing several of these checks should lower
confidence in the claim regardless of the headline number.

**Related** — [[claim--kots-electrostimulation-strength-claims-not-replicated]],
[[framework--clinical-physiological-effects-of-electrostimulation]].

# Seventeen Claimed Clinical and Physiological Effects of Electrostimulation, With Their Original Citations

**What it is** — The authors catalog electrostimulation's (ES) reported applications and
effects, each with cited sources: (1) increase in muscle strength, greatest in the weakest
or most unfit subjects, with ES alone at best producing gains "similar to or smaller than
those of voluntary exercise", though with periodised exercise programmes ES "appears to
increase the strength of competitive athletes in some instances" (Francis, 1982; Kots &
Chwilon, 1971; Matteson, 1984; Reding, 1973), "although these changes may have been the
indirect result of some of the other effects of ES" (PDF p. 222, printed p. 211); (2)
re-education of faulty muscle-action patterns, e.g. chondromalacia patellae, tennis elbow,
"frozen shoulder" (Eriksson, 1981; Godfrey et al, 1979; Johnson et al, 1977; Nirschl &
Sobel, 1981); (3) facilitation of contraction when voluntary contraction is blocked by
disuse, pain or injury, reducing tissue wasting; (4) increased muscular and systemic
endurance from prolonged sub-maximal ES, with low-frequency (under 15 Hz), long-duration
(24-hour) continuous stimulation or cross-innervation shown in animal studies to shift
fast-twitch fibres toward a more aerobic, fatigue-resistant profile (Jolesz & Sreter, 1981;

# Seventeen Claimed Clinical and Physiological Effects of Electrostimulation, With Their Original Citations

**What it is** — The authors catalog electrostimulation's (ES) reported applications and
effects, each with cited sources: (1) increase in muscle strength, strongest in
incapacitated, unfit or weakest subjects, with ES alone at best matching or trailing
voluntary exercise, though periodised programmes combining ES with training sometimes
increased competitive athletes' strength (Francis, 1982; Kots & Chwilon, 1971; Matteson,
1984; Reding, 1973); (2) re-education of faulty muscle-action patterns, e.g. chondromalacia
patellae, tennis elbow, "frozen shoulder" (Eriksson, 1981; Godfrey et al, 1979; Johnson et
al, 1977; Nirschl & Sobel, 1981); (3) facilitation of contraction when voluntary contraction
is blocked by disuse, pain or injury, reducing tissue wasting; (4) increased muscular and
systemic endurance from prolonged sub-maximal ES, with low-frequency (under 15 Hz),
24-hour continuous stimulation shown in animal studies to shift fast-twitch fibres toward a
more aerobic, fatigue-resistant profile (Jolesz & Sreter, 1981; Pette, 1984; Pette & Vrbova,
1985; Salmons & Vrbova, 1969; Salmons & Henriksson, 1981); (5) increased speed of
contraction from long-term, higher-frequency (over 40 Hz) ES, improving reaction time and
decreasing time-to-peak-tension of fast-twitch fibres (Fleury & Lagasse, 1979; Salmons &
Vrbova, 1967, 1969); (6) increased local blood supply, with measured increases from about
20% to over 200%, greatest below roughly 30 Hz (Currier et al, 1986; Richardson, 1981;
Wakim et al, 1948; Wakim, 1953); (7) a massage-like pumping action on venous/lymphatic
return; (8) pain relief via TENS, using low-frequency (50-100 Hz) stimulation without
contraction for superficial pain, or short, high-intensity bursts (1-150 Hz) with
contraction for deeper pain; (9) reduction of protective muscle spasm and spasticity; (10)
promotion of relaxation and recuperation, attributed to central endorphin/enkephalin
release, used by Russian athletes for post-training recuperation and to aid sleep onset even
with mild thigh-only stimulation; (11) increased range of movement, used alongside PNF
mobilisation; (12) reduction of non-infectious swelling; (13) halting or slowing mild to
moderate scoliotic curvature with ES applied to specific back muscles (Axelgaard et al,
1983; Friedman et al, 1982; Kots & Chwilon, 1971; Schultz et al, 1981); (14) preferential
recruitment of the largest-diameter motor axons first, the reverse of natural recruitment
order, making them a supplementary route to axons that are hard to activate under normal
training (Enoka, 1988); (15) an acute strength increase after a single session: Alon (1985),
studying 14 subjects, found one experimental ES session produced a mean 13% increase in
quadriceps strength; (16) improved metabolic economy: Ratov & Kryazhev (1986) found
electrically stimulating the quadriceps during cycling and speed skating reduced oxygen
consumption by 10-17% and extended time-to-fatigue by 15-20%, and treadmill running with ES
reduced oxygen consumption by about 10%, or by about 5% if the stimulated muscles had just
performed the work; (17) increased contractile speed of skeletal muscle via phasic-type ES.
(PDF pp. 221-224, printed pp. 210-213, "4.2.1.3 Clinical Applications of
Electrostimulation.")

**Why it works** — The authors give a distinct proposed mechanism for each effect
(catalogued above per item) rather than one unifying mechanism; several (items 4-5, 14, 17)
are tied to fibre-type recruitment and conversion, while others (6-13) are tied to blood
flow, central neurochemistry, or mechanical pumping action. Inference: no single theory in
this passage ties all seventeen together; the authors' own attempt at unification is the
separate MACS/MICS theory (see
[[claim--macs-mics-integrated-theory-of-electrostimulation]]).

**When to apply** — Use this as a reference catalog when deciding whether ES could serve a
specific, narrow purpose (e.g. swelling reduction, pain relief, post-training recuperation)
distinct from strength development, which the authors treat as ES's weakest and most
contested claimed benefit (see
[[claim--kots-electrostimulation-strength-claims-not-replicated]]). Inference: for Athletic
Medicine or Applied Performance settings, items 6-13 (blood flow, pain, spasm, swelling,
recuperation, ROM) map most directly onto standard rehabilitation and recovery use cases,
while items 1-5, 14-17 (strength, endurance, speed, recruitment, metabolic economy) are the
more contested performance-training claims.

**When NOT to apply** — Each item rests on citations from roughly 1948-1988, mostly single
studies or small samples (e.g. Alon's 13% figure is from 14 subjects, one session); none are
independently re-validated within this ingest. Item 4's fibre-type conversion evidence is
from animal (cross-innervation, continuous 24-hour stimulation) studies, not directly
transferable to standard clinical ES dosing. Do not treat this list as equally strong
evidence across all seventeen items; some (blood flow, pain relief, swelling) have broader
citation support here than others (scoliosis, acute strength).

**Example** — Inference: a post-training recovery application (item 10, low-current
stimulation to aid relaxation and sleep onset) is a narrower, better-supported use case than
citing this same list to justify ES as a primary strength-training tool (item 1, contested
above); a practitioner should not conflate the two when deciding whether to add ES to a
program.

**Related** — [[claim--kots-electrostimulation-strength-claims-not-replicated]],
[[heuristic--nine-reasons-electrostimulation-research-conflicts]],
[[claim--macs-mics-integrated-theory-of-electrostimulation]].

# The Authors' MACS/MICS Theory of Electrostimulation: Macro-Current as Stressor, Micro-Current as Non-Stressor

**What it is** — The authors state that "electric currents as much as 1000 times smaller
than that of all the traditional physical therapy modalities can be far more successful than
the latter in achieving many of the benefits outlined in the previous section", and that
currents as low as 10 microamps pulsating at 0.1 to 400 Hz, too weak to cause contraction,
block pain signals or cause local heating, have an "effectiveness and safety [that] is often
superior in many applications to that of faradism, interferentialism and conventional TENS"
(Matteson & Eberhardt, 1985) (PDF p. 224, printed p. 213). From this they propose an
integrated theory, introduced with "it appears as if": macroelectric cellular stimulation
(**MACS**, currents exceeding one milliamp) acts as a physiological stressor producing the
alarm response described by Selye (1975). They cite Eriksson et al (1981), who found the
acute effects of traditional ES similar to those of intense voluntary exercise, and Gambke et
al (1985), who found in animal studies that long-term MACS causes some muscle fibres, mainly
FT fibres, to degenerate a few days after ES and be replaced by new fibres from
satellite-cell proliferation. Applying Selye's model (see 1.16), the body would draw on its
superficial adaptation energy stores to adapt to MACS by increasing strength or endurance, or
by fibre-type transformation; if the ES is too intense, too prolonged or inappropriately
used, adaptation might not occur or might increase the proportion of slow-twitch fibres and
reduce strength, and "excessively demanding MACS conceivably might cause the body to draw on
its deep adaptation energy and lead to permanent tissue damage" (PDF p. 225, printed p. 214).
Microelectric cellular stimulation (**MICS**, currents below one milliamp) "would not act as
a stressor"; it is said to elicit biochemical changes tied to "resonant attunement of the
stimulus to cellular and subcellular processes" (p.214). The supporting findings cited: Becker
and colleagues on sub-threshold modulation of electric fields across nerve and glial cells,
including accelerated wound healing and partial limb regeneration in amphibians and rats
(Becker, 1974; Becker & Marino, 1982); Nordenstrom's "closed electric circuits" carrying ionic
flow along blood vessels (Nordenstrom, 1983); Pilla's (1974) membrane-signalling model and
cellular "windows" that open most effectively to certain frequencies, pulse widths and
amplitudes (Pilla, 1981); Rodan et al (1978), who found 5 Hz ES stimulated DNA synthesis in
chick cartilage cells and rat bone by as much as 27% (but not in chick skin fibroblasts or rat
spleen lymphocytes) 4-6 hours after 15 minutes of ES; and Cheng et al (1982), who found
50-1000 microamp currents increased rat tissue ATP by 300-500% and amino-acid transport and
protein synthesis by as much as 40%, while currents above one milliamp depressed ATP and
protein synthesis (traditional ES usually exceeds 20 milliamps, at which the depression is
"nearly 50%") (PDF p. 224, printed p. 213).

Safety statements attached to the theory. The authors state "It is generally entirely safe
to apply MICS anywhere on the body" (p.214) and that MICS "cannot produce overtraining or
injury" (PDF p. 226, printed p. 215). They give no safety data; the claim follows from their
MICS model. They also state that "Under no circumstances should MACS be applied across the
brain, as it can cause serious harm", and that "It is generally not advisable to apply any
form of ES to epileptics, pregnant women, cardiac patients or persons with heart pacemakers"
(PDF p. 225, printed p. 214). A counterweight in the same section: "routine or frequent use
of accelerated methods of restoration can impair the natural ability of the body to
recuperate and adapt; it is sometimes important to allow the body to undergo partial or
unaccelerated restoration to facilitate the supercompensatory response (Siff & Yessis,
1992)" (PDF p. 227, printed p. 216). (PDF pp. 224-227, printed pp. 213-216, "4.2.1.4 Further
Research Findings", "4.2.1.5 An Integrated Theory of Electrostimulation" and "4.2.1.6 The Use
of Electrostimulation in Training.")

**Why it works** — This is the authors' own proposed synthesis. Inference: it rests on two
threads of different standing: (a) the point that MACS-range ES acts as a training stressor
subject to dose-response and overtraining risk (the Selye, Eriksson and Gambke citations);
and (b) a set of bioelectric claims (Becker's regeneration work, Nordenstrom's closed
circuits, Pilla's cellular windows) offered as a general theory of cell communication.
Inference: thread (b) has not, as far as this ingest has checked, entered mainstream
sports-science or clinical practice; no named source for that judgment is given here. The
authors use the limits of the action-potential model as an argument for their alternative:
"little is known about electrical fields at the subcellular level", and classical theory
does not explain "the repair of fractures, the healing of wounds and reduction of
thrombosis" (PDF p. 221, printed p. 210).

**When to apply** — Inference: the (a) thread, that macro-current ES functions as a stressor
requiring progressive dosing rather than a fixed protocol, is consistent with basic
training-load principles and does not depend on accepting thread (b). The authors' own
dosing statement: an athlete who benefits from MACS "should not assume that increased dosage
will lead to further improvement. The contrary may well prove to be true" (p.214). Inference:
do not use this entry to justify low-current "microcurrent" devices for performance or
healing claims without independent, modern verification outside this book.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked `contested`. Inference: several supporting claims in thread
(b) (glial cells acting like semiconductors, Nordenstrom's closed circuits, "resonant
attunement" as the operative principle of MICS) are not treated here as independently
replicated physiology, and this entry does not verify them against current literature. The
Rodan (1978) and Cheng (1982) findings are animal and cell studies (chick cartilage, rat bone,
rat tissue) at narrow current ranges; they do not establish that MICS produces general
"adaptation, growth and repair" effects in human athletes. The MICS safety claims (p.214,
p.215) come without safety data. Inference: "MACS" and "MICS" appear to be the authors' own
terms for this section.

**Example** — Inference: a practitioner who reads that 10-microamp devices are more effective
and safer than faradic stimulators should recognise that the claim is the authors' (citing
Matteson & Eberhardt, 1985, p.213) and that its explanation rests on thread (b) (Becker,
Nordenstrom, Pilla), and should keep the authors' own contraindications (p.214) in force
whatever the device.

**Related** — [[framework--clinical-physiological-effects-of-electrostimulation]],
[[heuristic--nine-reasons-electrostimulation-research-conflicts]] (item 9, the alternative
physiological models),
[[heuristic--electrostimulation-sequencing-dosage-and-safety-practicalities]] (the practical
dosing limits and safety rules).

# Practical Rules for Integrating Electrostimulation Into a Programme: Sequencing, Electrode Placement, Dose Limits

**What it is** — "Several researchers (Purvin, Deniskin, Khodykin)", cited without dates,
studied how electrostimulation (ES) combines with other training means. They found that ES
first, followed by plyometrics, produces a greater training effect than the reverse order;
"a still larger effect was obtained by using ES and plyometrics concurrently with heavy
resistance exercise", while the ES and plyometric combination had its smallest training
effect during periods of complete or partial rest (PDF pp. 225-226, printed pp. 214-215).
Electrode placement matters: adjacent (close) attachment localises the contraction and keeps
it fairly superficial, while distant attachment (one electrode at a remote or fairly neutral
site) produces a more extensive, deeper contraction; electrode gel or weak saline solution is
needed for comfortable conduction, and skin irritation or prickliness "invariably" results
from the gel drying out. Electrodes may be placed directly over important nerves, but "the
intensity of the ensuing contraction can be harmful" and this method "should be restricted to
use by experienced physical therapists" (PDF p. 226, printed p. 215). On dosing: it is
"generally not advisable to apply more than 5-10 minutes of intense ES per major muscle
group, due to the associated tissue necrosis and prolonged soreness that may follow in the
days after treatment"; biofeedback TENS devices that monitor cellular electrical
characteristics and adjust parameters automatically limit the possibility of overstimulation
or cell damage (p.215). An athlete who benefits from MACS (macro-current ES) "should not
assume that increased dosage will lead to further improvement. The contrary may well prove
to be true" (PDF p. 225, printed p. 214; see
[[claim--macs-mics-integrated-theory-of-electrostimulation]]).

Safety rules, stated by the authors (PDF p. 225, printed p. 214): "Under no circumstances
should MACS be applied across the brain, as it can cause serious harm." "It is generally not
advisable to apply any form of ES to epileptics, pregnant women, cardiac patients or persons
with heart pacemakers." They also state that it is "generally entirely safe to apply MICS
anywhere on the body" (p.214), a claim for which they give no safety data (see the MACS/MICS
entry).

The authors' closing recommendation is that "the untutored reader is not encouraged to use
ES, since it requires considerable theoretical and practical training for its safe and
effective application"; casual users generally note sporadic or short-term progress and stop
after a few months. "In several countries (such as the USA), ES devices generally may not be
sold to the public or used commercially or therapeutically on any clients by anyone who is
not trained in medicine or physiotherapy" (PDF p. 227, printed p. 216). Inference: this is
the authors' statement at the time of writing; current regulation is not checked here.
(PDF pp. 225-227, printed pp. 214-216, "4.2.1.5" and "4.2.1.6 The Use of Electrostimulation
in Training.")

**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism for the sequencing or placement findings.
For the dose limit they cite tissue necrosis and prolonged soreness (p.215). Inference:
potentiation from ES before plyometrics, and current path between electrodes, are plausible
but not stated. Inference: the sequencing result can be read as an instance of the book's
training-order argument (see [[framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order]]).

**When to apply** — Use the sequencing finding (ES before plyometrics gave a larger effect

# Inertial (Flywheel) and Elastic Resistance: Different Force Profiles From Free Weights, Each With Its Own Limitation

**What it is** — The authors note that specialised equipment for training against a load's
inertia (rather than its weight) is rarely used, despite the concept warranting more serious
attention. Two solutions are given: applying force against a horizontal wheel or a
suspended, pendulum-like load, or spinning a heavy flywheel ergometer with the arms or legs
(Fig 4.4, elbow-flexion flywheel device, Verkhoshansky 1977). A flywheel device's moment of
inertia can be varied to change the speed-of-contraction demand, and it can be used several
ways: accelerating against high inertia, using the wheel's momentum to compel a certain
movement cadence, or opposing the wheel's angular momentum via eccentric muscle action to
decelerate it, with these methods combinable in short or mixed bursts. Elastic bands are
treated as a separate special case: resistance follows Hooke's Law (F = kx, where k is the
spring constant and x is extension), so elastic force starts at zero and rises with range of
movement; the authors state plainly that "elastic materials should not be used for
developing starting-strength in ballistic movements or for developing explosive-strength,"
because those qualities need force available from the very start of the movement, which
elastics cannot supply. For strength-endurance over a selected range, however, an elastic
band's length and elasticity can be chosen so its resistance changes minimally over the
working range, a method used by swimmers to develop pulling strength-endurance (Fig 4.5,
Verkhoshansky 1977). Resistance at "sticking points" can be reduced by moving toward the
band's attachment point, or increased by moving away from it; resistance can also be varied
across the full range by accelerating free weights through a decreasing-resistance portion
of the lift (so-called Compensatory Acceleration Training, see
[[framework--compensatory-acceleration-training]]) or by using dedicated variable-resistance
machines. (PDF pp. 219-220, printed pp. 219-220, "4.2.2 Resistance and Strength Training,"
Figs 4.4-4.5.)

**Why it works** — For flywheel/inertial devices, the mechanism is that resistance is
determined by the load's inertia (F = ma) rather than its weight (F = m(g+a)), so the
athlete can train speed of contraction against a resistance that does not exist at rest, only
once acceleration is applied, unlike a gravity-loaded free weight. For elastic bands, the
mechanism is Hooke's Law itself: resistance is proportional to extension, so it is
inherently near-zero at the start of the range and maximal at the end, the opposite loading
curve from what ballistic and explosive-strength work typically needs (high force available
immediately).

**When to apply** — Use flywheel/inertial devices when the training goal is speed of
muscular contraction against inertia specifically (per
[[framework--two-force-regimes-overcoming-weight-vs-inertia]]), varying moment of inertia to
adjust the demand, and consider eccentric-deceleration use of the same device for eccentric
overload. Use elastic bands specifically for strength-endurance work over a selected range
(the authors' cited example: swimmers' pulling strength-endurance), choosing band length and
elasticity to minimise resistance variation across that range, and use position along the
band (closer to or farther from the attachment) to manage sticking-point loading.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not use elastic-band resistance alone for developing
starting-strength or explosive-strength in ballistic movements; the authors state this
directly, since Hooke's Law resistance is lowest exactly when ballistic/explosive movements
most need force to be available. The flywheel and pendulum devices described are
purpose-built or improvised apparatus (a 1992 University of the Witwatersrand student
biomechanics project supplied the plyometric bench-press device shown nearby, Fig 4.6, a
related but separate kinetic-energy device); the authors give no standardised commercial
specification for the flywheel or pendulum devices described here.

**Example** — Inference: a swim coach building pulling strength-endurance with resistance
bands, per the authors' own cited example, should select a band whose resistance changes
little across the stroke's working range, rather than a stiffer band whose resistance would
spike sharply near full extension; a sprint or jump coach chasing starting-strength or
explosive-strength should not substitute elastic-band resistance for free weights or
inertial-device training for that specific quality.

**Related** — [[framework--two-force-regimes-overcoming-weight-vs-inertia]],
[[framework--compensatory-acceleration-training]].

# Inertial (Flywheel) and Elastic Resistance: Different Force Profiles From Free Weights, Each With Its Own Limitation

**What it is** — The authors note that specialised equipment for training against a load's
inertia (rather than its weight) is rarely used, despite the concept warranting more serious
attention. Two solutions are given: applying force against a horizontal wheel or a
suspended, pendulum-like load, or spinning a heavy flywheel ergometer with the arms or legs
(Fig 4.4, elbow-flexion flywheel device, Verkhoshansky 1977). "In the first example, one can
vary the amount of weight and in the second, the moment of inertia of the flywheel to affect
speed of contraction." Flywheel ergometers can be used several ways: "accelerating against
high inertia, using the heavy wheel to compel one to operate at a certain cadence, and
opposing the angular momentum via eccentric muscle action to decelerate the wheel", with
these methods combinable in short or mixed bursts. Elastic bands are treated as a separate
case: resistance follows Hooke's Law (F = kx, where k is the spring constant and x is
extension), so elastic force "begins from zero value and increases with movement range";
therefore, the authors state, "elastic materials should not be used for developing
starting-strength in ballistic movements or for developing explosive-strength". Inference:
those qualities need force available from the very start of the movement, which elastics
cannot supply. For strength-endurance over a selected range, however, an elastic band's
length and elasticity can be chosen so its resistance changes minimally over the working
range, a method "sometimes used by swimmers" to develop pulling strength-endurance (Fig 4.5,
Verkhoshansky 1977). Resistance at "sticking points" can be reduced by moving toward the
band's attachment point, or increased by moving away from it; resistance can also be varied
across the full range by accelerating free weights through a decreasing-resistance portion
of the lift (so-called Compensatory Acceleration Training, see
[[framework--compensatory-acceleration-training]]) or by using dedicated variable-resistance
machines. (PDF p. 230, printed p. 219, "4.2.2 Resistance and Strength Training," Figs
4.4-4.5.)

weight of the load and the speed of muscular contraction" (p.219). Inference: the athlete

ballistic and explosive-strength work needs.

speed of muscular contraction against inertia specifically (per
[[framework--two-force-regimes-overcoming-weight-vs-inertia]]), varying the moment of

demand, and consider "opposing the angular momentum via eccentric muscle action to
decelerate the wheel" (p.219) as a separate use of the same device. Use elastic bands specifically for strength-endurance work over a selected range
(the authors' cited example: swimmers' pulling strength-endurance), choosing band length and
elasticity to minimise resistance variation across that range, and use position along the
band (closer to or farther from the attachment) to manage sticking-point loading.

**Why it works** — The mechanism is straightforward Newtonian mechanics: F = m(g+a) versus F
= ma describe two different physical situations a muscle can be asked to produce force
against, and the authors' point is that a muscle's neuromuscular demand differs between
starting from a preloaded isometric-like state (weight-bearing) and starting from
essentially unloaded rest and having to generate speed against only inertia. The "large
gradient of acceleration-strength" in the weight-bearing case follows from force already
being non-zero (equal to the load's weight) at the instant motion begins, unlike the
inertia-only case, which starts from near-zero force.

**When to apply** — Use the preliminary-tension distinction (loaded-start vs
from-zero-start) to classify which exercises best target starting strength specifically:
per this framework, exercises that begin from essentially zero muscular tension (snatch,
clean-and-jerk, and by extension sprint starts, punches, throws) uniquely combine dynamic
strength, movement speed and starting-strength development, while loaded-start exercises
(squat, squat jump) do not train the speed of switching from rest to active state in the
same way. Use the weight-versus-inertia distinction to separate exercises meant to build
raw strength capacity (heavy squats, deadlifts) from those meant to build speed of
contraction against a light or unloaded resistance (medicine-ball throws, sprint
acceleration drills, punching).

# The Optimal Depth-Jump Drop Height Is 0.75-1.15 Metres: Maximal Power at the Low End, Maximal Force at the High End

**What it is** — Fig 4.7 (PDF p. 232, printed p. 221; Verkhoshansky, 1977) plots force, in
bodyweights, against time for three vertical jumps: (1) jumping from rest from a low squat,
(2) the usual jump with a dip or amortisation phase, (3) a jump after a depth jump from
0.4 m. The caption gives jump heights of 0.67 m, 0.74 m and 0.80 m respectively. Verified
against the page image (readings from the figure, approximate): curve 1 peaks early, about
1.4-1.5 BW at about 0.08-0.1 s, and ends about 0.3 s; curve 2 first drops below bodyweight
(about 0.6 BW at about 0.15 s), then peaks about 1.4 BW at about 0.5 s and ends about 0.8 s;
curve 3 peaks about 3 BW at about 0.1 s and ends about 0.25 s. Curves 1 and 2 have similar
peaks, and curve 2's is the later; only curve 3 is clearly higher and earlier.

Depth jumps from a range of drop heights (Fig 4.10, PDF p. 234, printed p. 223): the text
states that "maximal force (Fmax) increases up to a height of 1.15 metres, then diminishes
sharply, while movement time begins by changing insignificantly, then increasing sharply.
Maximum power and reactivity are achieved using a drop height of approximately 0.75 metres"
(PDF p. 233, printed p. 222). Verified against the page image (approximate): Fmax peaks near
1.1-1.15 m and falls sharply to 1.55 m; the figure also carries a Power curve, not named in
the caption, peaking about 0.75 m; RC peaks about 0.8 m; ground contact time t dips slightly
to a minimum about 0.75 m, then rises sharply. The authors conclude that the optimal range of
depth jumping for stimulating muscular activity is 0.75-1.15 metres, "because at the lower
end of this range the muscles are working at maximal power and at the upper end they are
working at maximal dynamic force". This finding "forms the basis for the recommendations for
using depth jumps in the training of advanced jumpers (Verkhoshansky 1963, 1964, 1966)",
though it is "preferable to err on the conservative side of using considerably lower jump
heights with anyone who is unused to this type of training and to strictly limit the volume
of this type of 'shock' training" (p.222).

The book states the result past 1.15 m two ways. The Fig 4.10 text says Fmax "diminishes
sharply" past 1.15 m; the next paragraph says further increases in height "significantly
decrease the magnitude of the dynamic parameters of the take-off", support time increases
quickly because the eccentric-concentric switch is lengthened, and "the maximum dynamic force
of take-off and the speed of muscular contraction stabilise and do not increase any further"
(p.222). The figure shows a sharp fall. Both are recorded; `contested` is set for this
internal contradiction. The take-off comprises amortisation (kinetic energy of the fall
absorbed, with increasing depth of knee flexion) and the thrust proper (fairly constant
speed of muscle contraction) (p.222).

Loaded depth jumps (Fig 4.9, PDF p. 234, printed p. 223; the caption is on the page image, not
in the text layer): after an unloaded depth jump (M = mass of athlete) and with an extra 10,
20, 30 and 40 kg. Verified against the page image: rebound height h2, force F and RC fall and
contact time t rises as load increases from M to M+40 kg. The text groups Figs 4.9 and 4.10
as showing the same tendency as the thrown-load experiment "under other conditions, although
these have their own peculiarities", and concludes "it is not beneficial to increase kinetic
energy by use of heavier loads" (p.222; see
[[claim--thrown-load-height-decreases-with-load-increases-with-drop-height]]). (PDF pp.
232-234, printed pp. 221-223, "4.2.3 Kinetic Energy and Strength Processes," Figs 4.7, 4.9,
4.10.)

**Why it works** — The authors' stated mechanism is elastic-energy storage during
amortisation and its release in the thrust (see
[[framework--kinetic-energy-stimulation-mechanical-basis-and-advantages]]), and for heights
past the optimum the lengthened switch from eccentric to concentric work (p.222). Inference:
at greater drop heights more of the force capacity may go to braking, which would fit force
rising to 1.15 m while power and reactivity peak earlier; the book does not state this.

**When to apply** — For advanced jumpers (Verkhoshansky 1963, 1964, 1966; p.222), use about
0.75 m when the training goal is maximal power and reactivity, and up to about 1.15 m when
the goal is maximal dynamic force, per this protocol. For athletes unused to depth-jump
training, start considerably lower and strictly limit volume, per the authors' caution.
Inference: this gives a citable historical anchor for programming depth-jump height, distinct
from the fixed 0.4 m depth-jump reactivity test already in this library (see

# Heavier Falling Loads Reduce Throw Height; Higher Falls Help Only Light Loads (Kinetic-Energy Throw Experiment)

**What it is** — A laboratory stand measured "the height attained by a load when a subject
threw it upward after it had first fallen from some height (from 0.5 to 3.0 metres)" (PDF
p. 232, printed p. 221). The load was 3.3, 6.6, 9.9 and 13.3% of the subject's maximum
isometric strength (Po) (Verkhoshansky, 1977); the figure labels the third load "10% Po"
where the text says 9.9% (PDF p. 233, printed p. 222). The authors summarise: "an increase in
kinetic energy caused by an increase in the mass of the load decreases the height to which a
load is thrown, but an increase in the distance through which a load falls increases the
height to which it is thrown (Fig 4.8a)" (p.222).

Fig 4.8a as read (PDF p. 233, printed p. 222; readings from the figure, approximate): the
x-axis (drop height h1) runs from 0 to 3 m, although the text gives 0.5-3.0 m. Only the 3.3%
Po curve rises throughout, from about 108 to about 128 cm. The 6.6% curve peaks about 108 cm
near 1.8 m, then dips to about 104 cm. The 10% curve peaks about 90 cm near 1-1.5 m and falls
to about 80 cm at 3 m. The 13.3% curve peaks about 69-70 cm near 1-1.2 m and falls to about
60 cm. Three of four loads peak and decline. The authors' summary says greater fall height
increases throw height; Fig 4.8a shows this only for 3.3% Po, while heavier loads peak at
about 1-2 m and decline. Both are recorded; `contested` is set for this contradiction between
the text and its own figure.

"A similar picture emerges from research on reactive ability (Fig 4.8b)" (p.222). Fig 4.8b
as read (approximate): reactive ability (RC) against the falling load's kinetic energy in
joules. The bold per-load curves mostly rise with kinetic energy: 3.3% Po climbs from about
3 to about 6.7 at about 7-8 J; 6.6% to about 5.2 at about 14 J; 10% to about 3.8-3.9 at about
17 J; 13.3% rises from about 1.3 to about 2.0 near 15 J, then dips slightly to about 1.8 at
20 J. Thin descending arcs are labelled 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 2.5 and 3.0 and join the load curves.
Inference: the figure gives these arcs no unit; given the text's 0.5-3.0 m fall range they
appear to join equal drop heights (m) across loads, so that at a fixed drop height a heavier
load, carrying more kinetic energy, gives a lower reactive coefficient. The authors conclude
"it is not beneficial to increase kinetic energy by use of heavier loads" and that "a better
means of increasing the thrust height" is needed (p.222). The book's parallel evidence is
loaded depth jumps (Fig 4.9, PDF p. 234, printed p. 223): with an extra 10-40 kg, rebound
height, force and RC fall and contact time rises (described in
[[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]]). (PDF pp. 232-233, printed pp.
221-222, "4.2.3 Kinetic Energy and Strength Processes," Fig 4.8.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no separate mechanism beyond the shared elastic-energy
logic of this section (see
[[framework--kinetic-energy-stimulation-mechanical-basis-and-advantages]]). A heavier load
carries more kinetic energy at a given fall height (KE = mgh, p.220). Inference: that extra
energy appears to exceed what the muscle can productively absorb and return within a short
amortisation phase, so throw height and reactivity fall off with load. Inference: this is
consistent with an optimal-loading range beyond which added mass mainly adds braking demand.

**When to apply** — Inference: use this as evidence against assuming "more kinetic energy
equals more training stimulus" in falling-load or catch-and-thrust exercises (e.g. weighted
plyometric throws, loaded catch-and-press devices). Within the tested range, lighter loads
gave greater throw height at every drop height, and raising the drop height helped the
lightest load throughout but helped heavier loads only up to about 1-2 m (Fig 4.8a).

**When NOT to apply** — This is a single-lab (Verkhoshansky, 1977) stand using a narrow load
range expressed relative to isometric strength (Po), not a standard external load; the
percentages and curve shapes should not be assumed to transfer to other exercises,
populations or load types without testing. The authors do not report the subject population
or sample size. Do not cite the book's summary sentence ("an increase in the distance ...
increases the height") without the Fig 4.8a qualification above.

**Example** — The book's own example is this experimental stand and its Fig 4.8 data; no
further example is added here.

**Related** — [[framework--kinetic-energy-stimulation-mechanical-basis-and-advantages]],
[[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]] (Fig 4.9 loaded depth jumps),
[[framework--reactivity-coefficient-and-depth-jump-test]] (Ch3.2.1, a related but distinct
reactivity-coefficient protocol using a fixed 0.4 m depth jump with externally added mass
rather than this section's variable fall-height, variable-load stand).

# Heavier Falling Loads Reduce How High They Get Thrown, but Falling From Higher Reduces It Less: The Kinetic-Energy Throw Experiment

**What it is** — A laboratory stand measured the height a subject could throw a load
upward after it had first fallen from a set height (0.5 to 3.0 metres), with load
expressed as a fraction of the subject's maximum isometric strength (Po): 3.3%, 6.6%,
9.9% and 13.3% of Po (Verkhoshansky, 1977). Verified against the page image (Fig 4.8a,
printed p. 222): as fall height (h1) increases from 0 to 3 metres, throw height (h2)
rises for every load, but the lighter loads (3.3% Po) reach a substantially greater throw
height at every fall height than the heavier loads (13.3% Po), and the heaviest load's
curve flattens and slightly declines at the greatest fall heights rather than continuing to
rise. The authors summarise: "an increase in kinetic energy caused by an increase in the
mass of the load decreases the height to which a load is thrown, but an increase in the
distance through which a load falls increases the height to which it is thrown." A similar
pattern appears for reactive ability (Fig 4.8b, reactivity coefficient plotted against the
falling load's kinetic energy in joules): verified against the page image, each load curve
(3.3%, 6.6%, 10%, 13.3% Po) is an inverted-U shape rising to a peak reactivity coefficient
then declining as kinetic energy increases further, with the peak's position and height
differing by load (the lightest, 3.3% Po, load reaches the highest peak reactivity
coefficient, around 7, at a moderate kinetic energy). The authors conclude "it is not
beneficial to increase kinetic energy by use of heavier loads," and that a better means of
increasing thrust height is needed. (PDF pp. 221-223, printed pp. 221-222, "4.2.3 Kinetic
Energy and Strength Processes," Fig 4.8.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no separate mechanism beyond the shared elastic-energy
logic already stated for this section (see
[[framework--kinetic-energy-stimulation-mechanical-basis-and-advantages]]): a heavier load
carries more kinetic energy at a given fall height (KE = mgh scales with mass), but that
extra energy appears to exceed what the muscle can productively absorb and return within a
short amortisation phase, so throw height and reactivity fall off rather than continuing to
rise with load. Inference: this is consistent with an optimal-loading phenomenon where
elastic-energy return and voluntary concentric contribution both have a productive range,
beyond which added mass mainly adds braking demand rather than usable stored energy.

**When to apply** — Use this as evidence against assuming "more kinetic energy equals more
training stimulus" when programming falling-load or catch-and-thrust exercises (e.g. weighted
plyometric throws, loaded catch-and-press devices): per this experiment, increasing the drop
height is a more productive way to raise thrust/throw height than increasing the load,
within the tested range (0.5-3.0 m fall heights, 3.3-13.3% of isometric strength as load).

**When NOT to apply** — This is a single-lab (Verkhoshansky, 1977) experimental stand using a
narrow load range expressed relative to isometric strength (Po), not a standard external
load; the specific percentages and the shape of the reactivity-coefficient curves should not
be assumed to transfer directly to other exercises, populations, or load types (e.g. a
