# Stimulating Muscle by Absorbing a Fall's Kinetic Energy: The Mechanics and Five Claimed Advantages Over Weighted Resistance

**What it is** — When a training device such as a barbell falls from a height and the
athlete's task is to actively stop it, then quickly thrust it upward (Fig 4.6, a purpose-built
plyometric bench-press device from a 1992 University of the Witwatersrand student
biomechanics project), the total muscular working force developed by eccentric amortisation
followed by active concentric work can be calculated as F = m(V1^2/2S1 + g) + m(V2^2/2S2 +
g), where V1 and V2 are the barbell's velocity at displacements S1 and S2 (derived from V^2 =
u^2 + 2as). Much of the falling apparatus's kinetic energy converts, during the amortisation
phase, into elastic energy used in the subsequent concentric work; excluding losses such as
heat and viscous damping as a first approximation, this elastic energy equals the kinetic
energy at the end of the fall (KE = mgh, where h is the fall height). Muscular force at the
eccentric-to-concentric switch is greater for a shorter amortisation phase and shorter
braking time, provided the goal is to thrust the apparatus at maximum speed immediately
after stopping it. The authors state the external mechanical stimulus here is "not so much
the weight (and its force of inertia) as the energy accumulated after its free-fall,"
distinguishing this from ordinary weighted resistance (see
[[framework--two-force-regimes-overcoming-weight-vs-inertia]]). Drawing on the vertical-jump
data in Fig 4.7 (see
[[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]]), the authors list five claimed
advantages of this stimulation method: (1) it develops maximal dynamic force very rapidly;
(2) the magnitude of that maximum is significantly larger than other methods produce; (3) a
large maximal force is achieved without additional resistance; (4) the eccentric-to-concentric
switch happens far more rapidly than with other methods; (5) the elastic energy accumulated
without additional resistance produces greater power and faster contraction in the thrust
phase, inferred from the greater jump height reached. (PDF pp. 220-222, printed pp. 220-221,
"4.2.3 Kinetic Energy and Strength Processes," Fig 4.6.)

**Why it works** — The authors' stated mechanism is elastic-energy storage and release during
the amortisation phase (the same mechanism underlying the shock method, see
[[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]]), combined with the mechanical
stimulation of proprioceptors at the instant of an abrupt stretch when a falling body is
stopped (citing Ramsey 1944; Hill 1955; Tweit et al 1963), which the authors say "creates the
conditions for developing starting strength and explosiveness of muscular action" that "no
heavy resistance exercise can imitate," because stimulating muscular activity with
significant extra resistance slows the eccentric-to-concentric transition.

**When to apply** — Use this framework's five advantages as the stated rationale for
programming falling-body/kinetic-energy stimulation (depth jumps, plyometric catches) rather
than purely weighted resistance when the specific goal is starting strength and explosive
strength, per the authors' own claim that these qualities are acquired slowly through
ordinary resistance training because they require unusually stressful, high-intensity
conditions that most popular resistance exercises do not reliably provide even though they
also start force development from rest.

**When NOT to apply** — The force formula (F = m(V1^2/2S1 + g) + m(V2^2/2S2 + g)) and the KE
= mgh approximation explicitly exclude heat generation and viscous damping "as a first
approximation," so treat it as a simplified model, not an exact measurement of muscular
force in vivo. The five advantages are presented as the authors' own summary claims from the
Fig 4.7 jump data (see
[[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]]), not as independently
replicated findings across other kinetic-energy-stimulation exercises; do not extend them
uncritically to every falling-load exercise without checking that exercise's own data.

**Example** — The book's own example is the depth-jump/plyometric-bench-press apparatus
described above (Fig 4.6); see
[[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]] for the specific numeric
findings this framework's advantages are drawn from.

**Related** — [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]] (Ch1, the shock-method
terminology and elastic-energy mechanism this framework builds on),
[[framework--two-force-regimes-overcoming-weight-vs-inertia]],
[[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]],
[[claim--thrown-load-height-decreases-with-load-increases-with-drop-height]].

# Four Ways to Stimulate Working Muscular Tension, and How They Map to the Rest of the Chapter

**What it is** — External muscular force is a product of voluntary effort, but voluntary
effort alone has limits; the authors classify how "stimulation of working force" is
supplied from outside that voluntary effort into four basic types: (1) muscular tension
produced by voluntary effort against external resistance, where the moving load's
resistance "accelerates and regulates the effector impulses to the muscles"; (2)
stimulation by the kinetic energy of a falling object or the body, where "the effort is
primarily reflexive"; (3) stimulation caused primarily by voluntary effort under conditions
where additional external mechanical stimulation is absent or limited; and (4) stimulation
of muscle "elicited or intensified involuntarily by means of external electrical current."
The authors group the first two as dynamic work and the third as isometric work; for the
first, increased stimulation comes from increasing the velocity of the preliminary fall of
the body or load; for the third, from "mobilising the athlete's voluntary resources."
Voluntary effort plays an important role in the first case, but is "insignificant" in the
second (the falling-body case), where the braking/amortisation mechanism produces a
protective reflex response faster than a voluntary sequence of actions can. This forms the
basis of plyometric training (see [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]]).
This four-way classification sets up the rest of the chapter's structure: type (4) is
covered next as 4.2.1 Electrostimulation, type (1) as 4.2.2 Resistance and Strength
Training, type (2) as 4.2.3 Kinetic Energy and Strength Processes, and type (3) as 4.2.4
Isometric Training. (PDF p. 218, printed p. 207, "4.2 Different Means of Strength
Development.")

**Why it works** — The authors' stated reason: afferent impulses elicited by mechanical
stimulation inform the central nervous system about the strength of the external
influence evoking muscular tension, and "the greater the intensity of the external
stimulus, the greater the muscle effector discharge, and the larger the external work
produced." Inference: this is a general afferent-feedback framing rather than a
mechanism specific to any one of the four types; the chapter's later sections give more
detailed, type-specific mechanisms (e.g. elastic energy storage for the falling-body case,
gradual overload for the resistance case).

**When to apply** — Use this as an organizing checklist when auditing a program's strength
means: does a given exercise stimulate tension primarily through external resistance,
through absorbed kinetic energy (a fall or catch), through sustained voluntary effort with
little external aid (isometric), or through externally applied electrical current? Mixing
means from more than one category (e.g. resistance plus electrostimulation) is a distinct
programming decision from staying within one category, and the chapter's later sections
(4.2.1 Electrostimulation, "Sports Functional Electrostimulation") discuss combining
categories explicitly.

**When NOT to apply** — Inference: this is the book's own convenience classification for
organizing chapter 4.2, not a claim that these four mechanisms are mutually exclusive
within a single exercise (a depth jump followed by a jump, for example, combines kinetic-
energy stimulation with subsequent voluntary resistance work). Do not treat the four-way
split as a measurement protocol; it carries no associated testing method here.

**Example** — Inference: a coach comparing a paused back squat (voluntary effort against
external resistance, type 1), a depth jump (kinetic energy of a fall, type 2), a wall sit
(sustained voluntary isometric effort, type 3), and a quadriceps NMES session (external
electrical current, type 4) is comparing four different stimulation mechanisms for the same
target muscle group, each covered by a different subsection of this chapter. This example
is not in the source.

**Related** — [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]] (Ch1, the falling-body
mechanism this framework's type 2 builds on); [[framework--precise-muscle-action-terminology]]
(Ch1, the mechanical regimes -concentric, eccentric, isometric- this framework's types map
onto at the muscle-action level, a distinct but adjacent classification).

# The Authors' MACS/MICS Theory of Electrostimulation: Macro-Current as Stressor, Micro-Current as Non-Stressor

**What it is** — The authors state that "electric currents as much as 1000 times smaller
than that of all the traditional physical therapy modalities can be far more successful than
the latter in achieving many of the benefits outlined in the previous section", and that
currents as low as 10 microamps pulsating at 0.1 to 400 Hz, too weak to cause contraction,
block pain signals or cause local heating, have an "effectiveness and safety [that] is often
superior in many applications to that of faradism, interferentialism and conventional TENS"
(Matteson & Eberhardt, 1985) (PDF p. 224, printed p. 213). From this they propose an
integrated theory, introduced with "it appears as if": macroelectric cellular stimulation
(**MACS**, currents exceeding one milliamp) acts as a physiological stressor producing the
alarm response described by Selye (1975). They cite Eriksson et al (1981), who found the
acute effects of traditional ES similar to those of intense voluntary exercise, and Gambke et
al (1985), who found in animal studies that long-term MACS causes some muscle fibres, mainly
FT fibres, to degenerate a few days after ES and be replaced by new fibres from
satellite-cell proliferation. Applying Selye's model (see 1.16), the body would draw on its
superficial adaptation energy stores to adapt to MACS by increasing strength or endurance, or
by fibre-type transformation; if the ES is too intense, too prolonged or inappropriately
used, adaptation might not occur or might increase the proportion of slow-twitch fibres and
reduce strength, and "excessively demanding MACS conceivably might cause the body to draw on
its deep adaptation energy and lead to permanent tissue damage" (PDF p. 225, printed p. 214).
Microelectric cellular stimulation (**MICS**, currents below one milliamp) "would not act as
a stressor"; it is said to elicit biochemical changes tied to "resonant attunement of the
stimulus to cellular and subcellular processes" (p.214). The supporting findings cited: Becker
and colleagues on sub-threshold modulation of electric fields across nerve and glial cells,
including accelerated wound healing and partial limb regeneration in amphibians and rats
(Becker, 1974; Becker & Marino, 1982); Nordenstrom's "closed electric circuits" carrying ionic
flow along blood vessels (Nordenstrom, 1983); Pilla's (1974) membrane-signalling model and
cellular "windows" that open most effectively to certain frequencies, pulse widths and
amplitudes (Pilla, 1981); Rodan et al (1978), who found 5 Hz ES stimulated DNA synthesis in
chick cartilage cells and rat bone by as much as 27% (but not in chick skin fibroblasts or rat
spleen lymphocytes) 4-6 hours after 15 minutes of ES; and Cheng et al (1982), who found
50-1000 microamp currents increased rat tissue ATP by 300-500% and amino-acid transport and
protein synthesis by as much as 40%, while currents above one milliamp depressed ATP and
protein synthesis (traditional ES usually exceeds 20 milliamps, at which the depression is
"nearly 50%") (PDF p. 224, printed p. 213).

Safety statements attached to the theory. The authors state "It is generally entirely safe
to apply MICS anywhere on the body" (p.214) and that MICS "cannot produce overtraining or
injury" (PDF p. 226, printed p. 215). They give no safety data; the claim follows from their
MICS model. They also state that "Under no circumstances should MACS be applied across the
brain, as it can cause serious harm", and that "It is generally not advisable to apply any
form of ES to epileptics, pregnant women, cardiac patients or persons with heart pacemakers"
(PDF p. 225, printed p. 214). A counterweight in the same section: "routine or frequent use
of accelerated methods of restoration can impair the natural ability of the body to
recuperate and adapt; it is sometimes important to allow the body to undergo partial or
unaccelerated restoration to facilitate the supercompensatory response (Siff & Yessis,
1992)" (PDF p. 227, printed p. 216). (PDF pp. 224-227, printed pp. 213-216, "4.2.1.4 Further
Research Findings", "4.2.1.5 An Integrated Theory of Electrostimulation" and "4.2.1.6 The Use
of Electrostimulation in Training.")

**Why it works** — This is the authors' own proposed synthesis. Inference: it rests on two
threads of different standing: (a) the point that MACS-range ES acts as a training stressor
subject to dose-response and overtraining risk (the Selye, Eriksson and Gambke citations);
and (b) a set of bioelectric claims (Becker's regeneration work, Nordenstrom's closed
circuits, Pilla's cellular windows) offered as a general theory of cell communication.
Inference: thread (b) has not, as far as this ingest has checked, entered mainstream
sports-science or clinical practice; no named source for that judgment is given here. The
authors use the limits of the action-potential model as an argument for their alternative:
"little is known about electrical fields at the subcellular level", and classical theory
does not explain "the repair of fractures, the healing of wounds and reduction of
thrombosis" (PDF p. 221, printed p. 210).

**When to apply** — Inference: the (a) thread, that macro-current ES functions as a stressor
requiring progressive dosing rather than a fixed protocol, is consistent with basic
training-load principles and does not depend on accepting thread (b). The authors' own
dosing statement: an athlete who benefits from MACS "should not assume that increased dosage
will lead to further improvement. The contrary may well prove to be true" (p.214). Inference:
do not use this entry to justify low-current "microcurrent" devices for performance or
healing claims without independent, modern verification outside this book.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked `contested`. Inference: several supporting claims in thread
(b) (glial cells acting like semiconductors, Nordenstrom's closed circuits, "resonant
attunement" as the operative principle of MICS) are not treated here as independently
replicated physiology, and this entry does not verify them against current literature. The
Rodan (1978) and Cheng (1982) findings are animal and cell studies (chick cartilage, rat bone,
rat tissue) at narrow current ranges; they do not establish that MICS produces general
"adaptation, growth and repair" effects in human athletes. The MICS safety claims (p.214,
p.215) come without safety data. Inference: "MACS" and "MICS" appear to be the authors' own
terms for this section.

**Example** — Inference: a practitioner who reads that 10-microamp devices are more effective
and safer than faradic stimulators should recognise that the claim is the authors' (citing
Matteson & Eberhardt, 1985, p.213) and that its explanation rests on thread (b) (Becker,
Nordenstrom, Pilla), and should keep the authors' own contraindications (p.214) in force
whatever the device.

**Related** — [[framework--clinical-physiological-effects-of-electrostimulation]],
[[heuristic--nine-reasons-electrostimulation-research-conflicts]] (item 9, the alternative

# Ratov's Functional Electrostimulation (FES): Timing the Current to the Athlete's Own EMG Signal During the Sport Skill Itself

**What it is** — In the 4.2.1 introduction the authors state that Ratov "has found that
functional electrical stimulation (FENS) can be particularly useful in improving sporting
performance". His techniques, developed from his PhD programme on the interrelation between
electrical stimulation and electromyography, use EMG signals from agonist and antagonist
muscles "to act as triggers or control mechanisms for electrical stimulation of muscles
directly involved in producing functional movements in sport". In his laboratory at the State
Central Institute for Sports Science in Moscow "he has successfully implemented these
neuromuscular stimulation methods in training athletes such as fencers, boxers, rowers,
shotputters and weightlifters" (PDF p. 219, printed p. 208).

In 4.2.1.6 the authors note that "little or no mention is made in the West of the
application of FES (Functional Electrostimulation) in sports training". In the West, FES or
its equivalent FENS (Functional Electroneural Stimulation) refers to ES that contracts the
muscles of spinally disabled patients who cannot voluntarily activate them. In Russia and
other Eastern European countries the terms can also mean applying ES to able-bodied athletes
during natural sporting movements "to intensify muscle tension at the most appropriate phases
of these movements". Professor Igor Ratov "stresses that this type of functional stimulation
is far more consistently successful than the passive methods attributed to Kots by his
Western supporters" (see [[claim--kots-electrostimulation-strength-claims-not-replicated]]).
Siff writes in the first person: "Work that I witnessed in his laboratory involved the use of
concurrent EMG recordings to phase the FES correctly into specific sporting movements, most
specifically to avoid producing spurious muscle tension or uncoordinated movement."
Eventually athletes learn to contract synchronously with the applied field "and thereby
produce greater strength, power and speed". This is sometimes called active
electrostimulation (ES applied to active muscles), as distinct from passive
electrostimulation (applied to relaxed muscles), the method most common in physical therapy
(PDF p. 226, printed p. 215). (PDF p. 219, printed p. 208, "4.2.1 Electrostimulation"; PDF
p. 226, printed p. 215, "Sports Functional Electrostimulation.")

**Why it works** — The stated logic: because the stimulus is phased by concurrent EMG into
the correct part of the movement, it avoids "spurious muscle tension or uncoordinated
movement" (p.215). Inference: no data (strength-gain percentages, EMG changes, performance
results) are reported for this method in these passages; the claim of superiority over
passive ES is Ratov's stated position as reported by the authors, not a cited experimental
comparison.

**When to apply** — Inference: relevant to anyone considering EMG-triggered or
movement-phased electrical stimulation for sport-specific training (as opposed to general or
isolated-muscle ES); the distinguishing feature to look for in any modern device or protocol
claiming this lineage is EMG-based triggering synchronised to the athlete's own movement,
not a fixed timing schedule.

**When NOT to apply** — Untested: no quantitative outcome data are reported for Ratov's
method in these passages, only a description of the approach, the authors' statement that he
"successfully implemented" it with named sport groups (p.208), and Siff's first-hand
observation (p.215). The claimed superiority over passive ES ("far more consistently
successful") is Ratov's own assessment as reported, not verified against a cited trial.
Inference: access to this method also depended on specialised laboratory equipment
(EMG-linked stimulators) not generally available. Inference: the only numbers from Ratov's
group in this section are Ratov & Kryazhev (1986), ES during cycling and speed skating (see
[[framework--clinical-physiological-effects-of-electrostimulation]], item 16, p.213).
Whether that work used EMG-triggered FES is not stated.

**Example** — The book's own example is Ratov's application with fencers, boxers, rowers,
shotputters and weightlifters (p.208), with the EMG phasing Siff witnessed (p.215); no
further example is added here.

**Related** — [[claim--kots-electrostimulation-strength-claims-not-replicated]],
[[case-study--reding-electrostimulation-protocol-siff-account]],
[[framework--clinical-physiological-effects-of-electrostimulation]] (item 16, Ratov &
Kryazhev 1986).

All 15 scoped Supertraining 4.2 (intro and 4.2.1-4.2.3) entries needed changes, and I made them. None was already fine. The lint shows no findings in any of the 15 files.

Before writing I read the source text for PDF pages 218-235 and opened all the figure pages, with zoomed crops of Fig 4.2, 4.7, 4.8a, 4.8b, 4.9 and 4.10. Every figure description I wrote comes from those images.

**Main fixes:**
- **Locators:** corrected to printed page + 11 in the six entries the review named. The four-mechanisms and Ratov locators now also cover PDF p. 219 / printed p. 208.
- **Figures:** Fig 4.7, 4.8a and 4.8b are re-described from the images. Fig 4.9 and the Fig 4.10 power curve are added.
- **Chikvadze 66%:** now attached to the weightlifter's lift, not the barbell jump.
- **Kots:** retitled, the invented "different protocol" detail is removed, and the book's "established" (p.208) vs "continue to disagree" (p.209) is recorded.
- **Reding:** the p.209 passage is now described as third person, Siff is described as the subject who received the ES (p.215), and the agonist/antagonist contradiction is recorded.
- **Safety rules from p.214:** MACS never across the brain; no ES for epileptics, pregnant women, cardiac patients or pacemaker users. These are now in both the safety heuristic and the MACS/MICS entry. The MICS safety claims are attributed to the authors, with a note that the book gives no safety data.
- **Other contradictions recorded:** Fig 4.3 caption vs text; Fmax "diminishes sharply" vs "stabilise"; Fig 4.8a vs its summary sentence; the "first case" fall-velocity slip.
- **Labels:** every unlabelled mechanism and prescription is now marked "Inference:". The recruitment entry's "Eric's baseline:" now quotes method-baseline.md line 61, including its "framework not Eric's own" tag.

**Where I departed from the review (7 items, all in the log):**
- **Two confidence changes to `contested`.** The depth-jump and thrown-load entries now read `contested`. In both, the book states the result in opposite directions (depth jump) or its text contradicts its own figure (thrown load). The brief's rule outranks the review's "`supported` is fine".
- **Ward & Shkuratova 2002 left out.** Only a cut-off abstract was available, so I could not confirm it reports non-replication. That abstract also says Kots claimed "up to 40%", against the book's "more than 20%". I noted this in the log, not in the entry.
- **Gregory & Bickel 2005 cited by PMID only (15794706).** The abstract confirmed the claim; the journal and pages the review gave could not be checked.
- **Minor figure readings:** the Fig 4.8b 13.3% curve rises from about 1.3 before it dips, and the Fig 4.7 curve 1 peak is nearer 0.1 s. The drop-height meaning of the thin arcs in Fig 4.8b is labelled "Inference:" because the figure gives them no unit.
- **MACS/MICS mainstream-status judgment** stays as "Inference:" with no named source.

**Could not verify:**
- whether Ward & Shkuratova reports non-replication
- the journal and pages for Gregory & Bickel
- any published source for how mainstream the MACS/MICS ideas are

**One problem outside my scope:** `_book.md` is now partly out of date and I did not edit it. Its lines 170-179 still say the Reding and Ratov entries are in Siff's own first-person voice, and its list of opened figures leaves out 4.9 and 4.10. Whoever owns `_book.md` needs to update that paragraph.

The final lint shows one issue, `_book.md` title/table dashes, which is the known false positive. An earlier run also flagged "round 2" in `claim--isometric-endurance-limits-and-recovery-phases.md`, which is outside my scope; it was gone on the re-run, and I did not touch that file. Both outputs are pasted in the log.
